issues.editorNote: Dial-up networks answer intruders with new hardware while Atari rebuilds its home-computer line and Lucasfilm prepares a new kind of computer game.
issues.morningLine: The telephone line is becoming both the personal computer’s doorway and its newest lock.

lead.headline: Telenet Locks the Dial-Up Door
lead.dek: A new device promises to bar unauthorized callers from computer systems reached over telephone lines.
body: WASHINGTON — GTE Telenet introduced a device Tuesday, May 15, designed to lock unauthorized users out of computer systems reached through telephone lines. The announcement turns the fast-growing worry over modem intrusion into a commercial hardware market.

Dial-up access is spreading beyond large institutions as lower-priced modems bring telecommunications within reach of homes and small offices. That convenience also means a computer can have a doorway far beyond the machine room, and network operators are now selling a lock for it.

The period report does not name a hacker crew or connect the product to a particular break-in. Its significance is broader: access control has become a product category, proof that remote computing is mature enough to demand both openness and defenses.

For home users, the same week’s magazine racks advertise comparisons of six modems below $100. The modem is moving from specialist equipment toward a mass-market peripheral just as the networks at the other end learn to question who is calling.

stories.headline: Atari Pledges a Sober XL Comeback
body: After a half-billion-dollar loss in 1983, Atari says its recovery will rest on profitability, reliability and products customers actually want. Chief executive James Morgan’s program includes a 40 percent overhead reduction and fewer premature promises.
The 600XL and 800XL are cast as the workhorses. A roughly $100 model 1064 module can expand the 16K 600XL to 64K, while specifications for the ambitious 1450XLD remain under review.
Software is part of the repair job: SynFile+, SynCalc and SynTrend, acquired from Synapse, bring database, spreadsheet, graphing and statistics tools to Atari’s 8-bit line at $99.95 each.

stories.headline: Lucasfilm Turns Its Cameras Toward Games
body: George Lucas’s company has entered the home video-game market, bringing film-production talent into interactive entertainment. The May 8 announcement was still fresh as this week began.

The venture stresses original play rather than a simple movie license. Its first Atari-computer projects would become Ballblazer, a futuristic split-screen sport, and Rescue on Fractalus!, a tense flight across an alien landscape.

stories.headline: Sub-$100 Modems Call the Home Office
body: The May issue of Computers & Electronics puts six modems costing less than $100 on its cover, a vivid sign that data communications is crossing a consumer price threshold.

Micro-to-mainframe access, bulletin boards and online services are becoming practical ambitions for a household machine. The bargain modem expands the audience—and makes the week’s Telenet security announcement feel less remote.

issues.editorNote: Lucasfilm's Games Group steps onto the home-computer stage with Ballblazer and Rescue on Fractalus!, while pens, tablets and sub-$100 word processors broaden what a family machine can do.
issues.morningLine: From a fractal alien mountain to the printed page, this is the week home computers learned new tricks.

lead.headline: Lucasfilm Brings the Force to Home Videogames
lead.dek: The film studio unveils Ballblazer and Rescue on Fractalus!, two Atari projects built around fresh technology and a cinematic sense of play.
body: SAN RAFAEL, Calif. — Lucasfilm publicly entered the home videogame market May 8, unveiling the first two projects from a Games Group nurtured through its collaboration with Atari. The announcement puts one of cinema's most famous technical workshops behind software intended for Atari 8-bit computers and the 5200 console.

Ballblazer turns a futuristic sport into a fast split-screen contest. Each player sees the arena from a first-person viewpoint while the computer produces a changing musical accompaniment, an unusually energetic pairing of action and sound for the home screen.

The companion project, then presented as Rescue on Fractalus!, places the player in a cockpit above an alien mountain range. Its terrain draws on Loren Carpenter's fractal graphics methods, allowing the machine to suggest an expansive, jagged landscape without storing every ridge by hand.

The two games remain previews rather than finished store releases, but they signal an ambitious new studio identity. Atari supplies hardware knowledge and marketing support; Lucasfilm supplies visual research, experimentation and the expectation that a computer game can stage a world rather than merely keep score.

stories.headline: Pens and Tablets Challenge the Keyboard
body: COMPUTE!'s May cover package asks readers to imagine pointing and drawing directly at the screen. Its survey of light pens and graphics tablets presents these devices as increasingly practical alternatives to typing commands.

A companion technical article explains how the devices report position, while the issue's Digital Palette feature and a 3-D surface-plotting program turn the idea into hands-on graphics work. The $2.95 magazine captures direct manipulation moving from laboratory curiosity toward the home desk.

stories.headline: Home Word Processing Drops Below $100
body: Atari is advertising AtariWriter, a 16K-compatible ROM cartridge, at under $100. The package offers search and replace, block movement, headers and footers, form letters, print preview, automatic page numbering and even an undo command.

Professional Software answers with WordPro 3 Plus/64 and SpellRight Plus for $99.95. The competing offers show serious writing tools becoming family-budget purchases, with mail merge and spelling assistance no longer reserved for an office system.

stories.headline: Atari Searches for a New Mission
body: Creative Computing describes Atari's new watchwords as profitability, reliability and creativity after a punishing year for the videogame business. The company must restore confidence while deciding how its home computers and game machines fit together.

The report arrives before the next great corporate turn: Warner still owns the consumer operation, but pressure for a workable plan is unmistakable. Lucasfilm's imaginative previews offer one example of the distinctive software Atari needs.

issues.editorNote: Europe's vast Hanover Fair points toward portable LCD machines and new 16-bit ambitions, while compatibility cards, music software and bulletin boards reshape the personal-computer world.
issues.morningLine: From Hanover's packed aisles to the local modem line, computers are getting smaller, more musical and more connected.

lead.headline: Hanover's 650,000 Visitors See the Portable Future
lead.dek: Epson lifts the lid on a lap-size LCD machine as Commodore signals a 16-bit business turn.
body: HANOVER, West Germany — One of Europe's largest computer fairs drew roughly 650,000 visitors this week, turning the exhibition floor into a vivid measure of how quickly electronic computing is moving from specialist rooms toward desks, briefcases and homes.

IBM assigned about 500 people to its own sprawling exhibit, but a much smaller machine supplied the most suggestive glimpse of the road ahead. Epson demonstrated a lap-size computer with a pop-up liquid-crystal display capable of showing eight lines of 80 characters.

The screen is modest beside a desktop monitor, yet the design makes portability more than a marketing word. A usable keyboard-and-display computer that can travel with its owner hints at a new class of personal machine for work beyond the office.

Commodore, meanwhile, showed an unnamed 16-bit system built around the Zilog Z8000. InfoWorld reported that Commodore was manufacturing the processor under license, a notable departure from the 6502-family chips behind its mass-market home computers.
Taken together, the exhibits reveal an industry testing two futures at once: lighter machines that follow their users and more powerful business systems reaching beyond the familiar 8-bit world.

stories.headline: Chuck Peddle Rides Back to Victor with the PlusPC
body: Chuck Peddle, the 6502 pioneer and founder of Victor Technologies, is returning to help the bankrupt computer maker manufacture and distribute its new PlusPC. The proposed arrangement still requires bankruptcy-court approval.

Victor bills the machine as IBM PC-compatible, an essential claim in a market rapidly organizing around that standard. Peddle stepped down as Victor's top officer in November 1983 but remains a major shareholder.

Working with consultant Chris Taylor, Peddle said the system was expected in time for July's National Computer Conference in Las Vegas. The plan gives Victor a possible route back into the industry's fastest-moving lane.

stories.headline: One Box, Two Computer Worlds
body: Rana's Quadlink card promises to let an IBM PC run Apple II software by placing a 6502 processor, 64K of memory, Applesoft ROM and Apple DOS 3.3 inside the PC chassis.

Rana says a cable change extends the idea to Columbia and Compaq compatibles. The company's Apple IIe add-on uses a dual-drive box, while Micro Craft's Dimension 68000 pursues the same compatibility problem with multiple coprocessors.
The convenience carries a price: Quadlink lists for $680, with one mail-order advertisement offering it for $485. Even so, the hardware shows how valuable existing software libraries have become.

stories.headline: Can a Computer Teach Music?
body: Programs for Commodore, Atari and Radio Shack computers are moving beyond games to teach notation, key signatures, rhythm and composition. Electronic Arts' Music Construction Set was tested on a Commodore 64 by classically trained musician Leslie Miller.

AtariMusic I and II have also appeared in studies where students learned without instructors. The experiments suggest that a home computer can become both an electronic score pad and a patient practice partner.

Gareth Loy of UC San Diego's computer-audio laboratory cautions that present machines remain limited in pitch accuracy and tone color. Improving low-cost synthesizers may narrow that gap, but musicians are not ready to dismiss the human teacher.

stories.headline: Early Macintosh Verdict: Brilliant, but Boxed In
body: Three months after launch, InfoWorld calls the Macintosh exceptionally easy to use, powerful and innovative. Its graphics and mouse-driven approach remain the machine's great attractions.

The review also asks for more than 128K of memory and a hard disk, while noting that the sealed case offers no internal expansion slots. A reader separately objects to the missing cursor keys and lack of letter-quality printing support.

Microsoft Multiplan for Macintosh earns praise as an improved version of InfoWorld's 1982 software product of the year. Strong applications may determine whether buyers accept the first Macintosh's tight limits.

undergroundDesk.headline: Computer-Access Law Meets the BBS Era
undergroundDesk.dek: Operators ask lawmakers to define electronic boundaries without treating every dial-up connection as malicious.
body: Proposed computer-access rules are colliding with the open, experimental culture of bulletin boards. The central dispute is how to define entry 'without authorization' when telephone numbers may be posted precisely because a system owner wants callers.

BBS operator John James uses a home board to circulate legislative information and argues that electronic communication increasingly matters to telecommuters. Anton Dovydaitis suggests that closed systems display an explicit electronic warning rather than leaving their status ambiguous.
The debate is about law, notice and intent, not intrusion technique. Its outcome may shape how online communities distinguish welcomed exploration from trespass.

issues.editorNote: Extra Edition: Apple’s compact IIc arrives carrying the vast Apple II library into a new era.
issues.morningLine: Apple II Forever: a familiar computer slips into a carryable new case.

lead.headline: Apple Puts the II in a Carrying Case
lead.dek: The $1,295 Apple IIc brings 128K, a built-in disk drive and nearly a decade of Apple II software into a compact 7.5-pound package.
body: SAN FRANCISCO — Apple Computer unveiled the Apple IIc on April 24 at its “Apple II Forever” dealer convention, putting the durable Apple II design into an ivory case small enough to carry by its handle. Even a 6.2-magnitude earthquake shaking Moscone Center could not upstage the week’s landmark personal-computer announcement.

At $1,295, the IIc includes a 1.02 MHz 65C02 processor, 128K of memory, Applesoft BASIC, a full-stroke keyboard and a built-in 5.25-inch floppy drive. The 7.5-pound machine is compact rather than truly cordless, but a broad set of ports accommodates a display, printer, modem, mouse or joystick and a second disk drive.

Compatibility is the strongest card in Apple’s hand. The company says roughly 90 percent of some 10,000 Apple II programs will run on the newcomer, letting families, schools and small offices keep their established software. Period reports say dealers placed more than 50,000 orders within hours.

The IIc also introduces Frog Design’s clean “Snow White” styling and extends Macintosh ideas to the older family through a $99 mouse bundled with MousePaint. Accessories range from a $199 green-screen monitor and $299 Scribe printer to a planned $600 flat display.

Apple is signaling that Macintosh and Apple II will advance together: one experiments with a graphical future, while the other carries a vast installed base into a friendlier shell. The IIc is evolutionary inside, but its combination of polish, portability and software breadth makes this an extra-edition week.

stories.headline: Apple II Forever, Apple III No More
body: Apple used the IIc debut to reassure dealers that Macintosh would not displace its established eight-bit line. The “Apple II Forever” theme turned compatibility and continuity into the convention’s rallying cry.

The same day brought the end of the troubled Apple III, Apple’s unsuccessful attempt to build a business successor to the II. The company now presents two clearer families: the profitable Apple II line for homes and schools, and Macintosh for its new graphical ambitions.
COMPUTE! later reported nearly two million Apple II-family machines sold, while Macintosh passed 70,000 in its first 100 days. Apple is pruning a failure while doubling down on its strongest names.

stories.headline: IBM’s PCjr Stumbles Out of the Gate
body: Reports immediately before this week say IBM’s PCjr is selling below expectations, sharpening the contest between two similarly priced family computers. Both the 128K PCjr and IIc offer a floppy drive, external power supply and ties to a larger software family.

Creative Computing finds the IIc keyboard markedly better, while noting the PCjr’s faster processor, side-bus expansion and cartridge slots. IBM’s machine retains the gravitational pull of the PC name, but its compromised keyboard and compatibility questions are proving costly.
Apple’s new entry makes ease of use and a proven library the center of the pitch. The home-computer contest will turn on what buyers can actually do after opening the box.

stories.headline: Software Becomes the Machine’s Magic
body: TIME’s April software cover calls programs “the magic carpet to the future,” capturing an industry shift from hardware novelty toward applications and usability. Apple’s IIc pitch makes the same argument through compatibility rather than raw processor power.
AppleWorks combines word processing, a database and a spreadsheet for the Apple II family. MousePaint, bundled with the IIc mouse, brings a Macintosh-style pointing interface to the older line.
The machine matters, but the library increasingly closes the sale. In 1984, useful programs—and the confidence that they will keep running—are becoming the most persuasive specification.

stories.headline: April’s Game Shelf Spans Machines
body: Computer Entertainer’s April issue finds a lively home-game shelf despite the console trade’s contraction. B.C.’s Quest for Tires and Fathom appear for Apple II, Oil’s Well for ColecoVision and Dragonhawk for Commodore 64.

Publishers continue to cross incompatible formats, searching for players on every popular machine. Arcade conversions share shelf space with original computer games, while reviews and mail-order listings help buyers navigate the crowded field.

Exact release days are often elusive, so these are April shelf sightings rather than claims of launch-day precision. They nevertheless show software variety remaining one of home computing’s strongest attractions.

lead.headline: Software Steps Into the Spotlight
lead.dek: TIME puts the programs inside the machine on its April 16 cover as applications, compatibility and ease of use begin deciding the personal-computer contest.
body: The personal-computer business has spent years selling the wonder of the machine itself. This week, the spotlight swings decisively to the programs that make those machines useful. TIME’s April 16 cover story, “The Wizard Inside the Machine,” calls software the magic carpet to the future and captures an industry learning that specifications alone do not close the sale.

That change can be seen on every shelf. Buyers now ask whether a computer can write a letter, keep accounts, draw a picture, teach a lesson or play the latest game—and whether files and programs will travel with them to the next machine. The contest is becoming one of libraries, compatibility and interfaces as much as processors and memory.

PC Magazine’s April 17 issue documents the application-rich IBM-compatible side of the market, while April’s COMPUTE! reaches across Commodore, Atari, Apple and IBM systems with ready-to-run programs. Together they show software becoming both the common language and the great dividing line of home computing.

For makers, the lesson is plain: a handsome box may win a demonstration, but a healthy catalog wins a household. For users, this new emphasis promises more practical machines—provided competing formats, disks and operating systems do not turn abundance into confusion.

stories.headline: Macintosh Meets the User-Group Crowd
body: COMPUTE! brings Apple’s new Macintosh before home-computer readers through a report on its Boston Computer Society demonstration. The compact 20-pound machine pairs an 8 MHz Motorola 68000 with a mouse, menus and a crisp graphical display.

The interface earns praise for direct manipulation, an Undo command and a remarkably tidy desktop. Yet the report also asks the question that follows every dazzling demonstration: what indispensable job will persuade ordinary buyers to spend $2,495?

MacWrite and MacPaint offer the first answer, turning words and pictures into visible objects on screen. The larger test will be whether independent developers can build a software shelf broad enough to make the unusual machine a standard.

stories.headline: Atari Sends Arcade Names to Rival Machines
body: Atari is treating its famous game catalog as portable property. COMPUTE! reports 12 releases under the ATARISOFT label for competing computers and consoles, carrying familiar arcade names beyond Atari hardware.

The strategy arrives as the console trade remains unsettled. Software sales on Commodore, Apple and Coleco machines give Atari another route to customers and acknowledge that a valuable game can outlive the box it first called home.
April’s Computer Entertainer tracks a busy field that includes B.C.’s Quest for Tires, Oil’s Well and Fathom. The shelf is fragmented, but the appetite for recognizable games remains strong.

stories.headline: PCjr and Macintosh Court the Newcomer
body: IBM and Apple are offering sharply different invitations to first-time buyers. The PCjr leans on the IBM name and PC family, while Macintosh asks users to learn a mouse-driven graphical vocabulary.
PCjr starts at $669, with the enhanced introduction configuration at $1,269; Macintosh arrives at $2,495. Price matters, but software support, expansion and the feel of daily work may matter more.

Early criticism of PCjr’s keyboard and limits gives Apple an opening, while IBM’s enormous software orbit remains a formidable advantage. The newcomer’s contest is already proving this week’s larger point: programs decide the value of the package.

issues.editorNote: Pictures are becoming commands: Sierra puts an icon-guided word processor on three rival home-computer families at once.
issues.morningLine: HomeWord turns six writing chores into pictures while Atari sends its arcade catalog onto competitors' machines.

lead.headline: HomeWord Brings Icons to Three Computer Camps
lead.dek: Sierra On-Line gives Apple, Commodore 64 and Atari owners the same $49.95 picture-guided word processor.
body: A filing cabinet, a printed page, a printer, a disorderly page with an arrow, a question mark and a floppy disk now stand between the home writer and the command line. Sierra On-Line has introduced HomeWord for the Apple, Commodore 64 and Atari families, using six pictured icons to guide the program's principal jobs.

The screen can be divided into working text, a miniature preview of the finished page and a status chart showing memory and disk space. COMPUTE! reports optional joystick control, outlining, boldface and underlining, block moves, file merging, headers and footers among the features.

The cross-platform release is as important as the interface. Apple, Commodore and Atari owners cannot exchange programs freely, yet Sierra is treating them as one mass audience and giving each the same visual vocabulary. The approach echoes the mouse-and-icon excitement surrounding Apple's Macintosh without requiring a new $2,495 computer.

At $49.95, HomeWord places an unusually approachable writing system on machines already sitting in dens and bedrooms. Its icons do not abolish the keyboard, but they make a practical case that everyday software can explain itself with pictures rather than a memorized thicket of commands.

stories.headline: Atari's Games Defect to the Competition
body: Atari has released twelve familiar games for competing computers and consoles under the ATARISOFT label. Centipede, Defender, Dig Dug, Donkey Kong, Pac-Man, Robotron and Stargate head a list that reaches Apple II, IBM PC, Commodore, TI, ColecoVision and Intellivision buyers.

The move is a striking admission after the videogame shakeout: Atari's characters and arcade names may earn more when they travel beyond Atari hardware. Suggested prices run $34.95 for computer disks, $44.95 for computer cartridges and $40.95 for ColecoVision or Intellivision editions.

stories.headline: War Games Grow Up on the Commodore 64
body: Strategic Simulations is widening the C64 library with Battle for Normandy and Tigers in the Snow, two $39.95 historical simulations that ask players to command campaigns rather than merely chase a score. Both provide a solitaire option and period campaign detail.

Carrier Force goes further on Apple and Atari at $59.95, modeling four Pacific carrier battles with individual ships and aircraft, weather, visibility, time of day and imperfect sightings. Together the releases show serious computer war gaming moving across the same fragmented machine market as arcade conversions.

stories.headline: The $100 Home Computer Is No Longer a Fantasy
body: Mail-order advertising in April's computer press lists the VIC-20 at $79.95 and the Atari 600XL at $139.95, or $99.95 after rebate. A Commodore 64 appears at $189.95. These are dealer offers, not manufacturers' list prices, and availability may change.

The falling entry price extends to communications: a VIC 1600 modem is advertised at $59.95 and a Commodore 1650 at $109.95. A complete home-computing setup remains costlier once storage and display are included, but the first machine—and a doorway to bulletin boards—is rapidly becoming an impulse-scale purchase.

stories.headline: Color Graphics Become a $39.95 C64 Tool
body: Sophisticated Software's Grafix-Artist gives Commodore 64 owners a high-resolution color drawing package controlled by a special command language or joystick. The publisher proposes program screens, storyboards, design layouts and advertising displays.

Grafix-Artist lists for $39.95; a separate $29.95 Grafix-Printer utility transfers the high-resolution work to paper. The pair reflects a growing market for tools that turn an inexpensive home machine into a small creative workstation.

issues.editorNote: Two very different machines reach the same buyer this spring, and the trade press finally puts them side by side.
issues.morningLine: IBM's Peanut and Apple's Macintosh go head to head on the newsstand while Atari sells its arcade library to everybody else's hardware.

lead.headline: The Peanut Meets the Mac: IBM and Apple Fight for the Next Home Buyer
lead.dek: TIME's April 2 report frames two incompatible visions of personal computing, one betting on compatibility, the other on the mouse.
body: The comparison that dealers have been making informally since January reached the national press this week. In its April 2 technology report, TIME set IBM's PCjr against Apple's Macintosh and described the two as new entries battling for attention from the same undecided buyer. The deck put it plainly: new entries from IBM and Apple battle for attention.

IBM's approach is continuity. The PCjr is an 8088-class machine sold in 64K and 128K configurations, extending the DOS world downward into the family room with better color and sound than the office PC offers. The strategy assumes buyers want the thing their employer already uses, only cheaper. The execution has been the problem: the infrared chiclet keyboard drew ridicule from the first demonstrations, and the machine's compatibility with the PC software library is incomplete enough that dealers must check titles case by case.

Apple's approach is discontinuity. The Macintosh puts a Motorola 68000 behind a built-in nine-inch monochrome display, packs 128K of memory and a 400K three-and-a-half-inch floppy into a case a clerk can carry with one hand, and ships a mouse as standard equipment rather than an accessory. Windows, icons and pull-down menus are not options in the Macintosh; they are the only way in. The list price is $2,495.

The two machines therefore ask the buyer a question the industry has avoided since the Apple II: is a personal computer a smaller version of the office machine, or a different kind of appliance altogether? IBM's answer protects an installed base and a software catalog worth thousands of titles. Apple's answer discards both and asks the customer to trust that pointing at pictures beats typing commands.

Neither answer has been settled by sales. What the week established is that the trade has stopped treating the two as separate stories. For the rest of 1984, every home-computer purchase decision will be argued in these terms.

stories.headline: Atari Invades Rival Machines With a Dozen Atarisoft Games
body: Atari has released twelve of its games for competing computers and videogame consoles under a new software label, ATARISOFT, COMPUTE! reports in its April issue. The line puts arcade properties long identified with Atari hardware onto the Commodore 64, VIC-20, Apple II, IBM PC, ColecoVision and TI-99/4A, depending on the title.

The move is an admission with a price tag attached. Atari's console business has spent a year contracting, and the company's most durable asset is no longer its hardware but the names on its cartridge labels. Selling those names to owners of rival machines converts a shrinking hardware franchise into a software one.

For the shopper the effect is immediate and slightly disorienting: familiar Atari boxes now sit on the Commodore shelf. For the industry it marks something larger. Software rights and recognizable games are becoming separable from the manufacturer that first shipped them, and the cartridge is no longer a proof of loyalty to any one machine.

stories.headline: PC Boom Turns Into a Stock-Market Crapshoot
body: John Case's analysis for Inc., published April 1, looks past the product announcements at the investors funding them and finds a wreck. “If you're a stockholder in the personal computer business, you've probably had your head handed to you by now,” Peter Wright, vice president of Gartner Group Advisory Inc., told the magazine.

The piece treats personal-computer investing as a contest shaped by IBM's gravitational pull, price cuts that arrive faster than inventory turns, and genuine uncertainty about which vendors will still be shipping in two years. A crowded field of machines is not the same thing as a crowded field of survivors.

Read alongside the week's launch coverage, the analysis supplies the counterweight. The same spring that produces the PCjr, the Macintosh and the Mindset is producing a shakeout, and the two facts are not in tension. They are the same fact seen from the showroom and from the ticker.

stories.headline: Mindset Pushes PC Graphics Beyond the IBM Mold
body: BYTE's April issue lists the Mindset personal computer among its notable contents, and the machine deserves the attention for reasons that have nothing to do with spreadsheet compatibility. It runs MS-DOS on an Intel 80186, but it is not a conventional full clone of the IBM PC.

The difference is custom graphics hardware. The Mindset supports 320-by-200 graphics with sixteen simultaneous colors chosen from a 512-color palette, with hardware assistance for drawing and animation rather than the software-only redraw that slows other MS-DOS machines. Optional equipment allows work with NTSC video input and output, aiming the system at titling and graphics production.

Surviving service documentation dated April 1984 confirms the system was entering supported commercial use this spring. Whether the market rewards a graphics-minded MS-DOS machine is another question, and one the same week's business coverage suggests will be answered harshly.

stories.headline: Jobs Sells the Macintosh as a Mission, Not Just a Machine
body: Joseph P. Kahn's profile of Steven Jobs, published April 1 by Inc., catches Apple's chairman before an audience in Boston's John Hancock Hall running a tightly staged audiovisual presentation. The subject is a computer; the register is evangelical.

The profile supplies period texture the specification sheets cannot. Apple is not merely selling a 68000 and a mouse for $2,495. It is selling a claim about how ordinary people should meet a computer, and the pitch is delivered with the conviction of someone who expects to be proved right in public.

issues.editorNote: Extra Edition: a newly independent AT&T carries Bell Labs Unix into direct competition with the established computer makers.
issues.morningLine: Unix steps onto the commercial main stage while microcomputer shelves fill with new drives, games and sharper enforcement against counterfeit tapes.

milestone.title: AT&T enters the general-purpose computer business with its Unix-based 3B line
milestone.note: The newly divested telephone giant's March 27 market entry put Bell Labs' Unix and AT&T-designed 32-bit hardware into direct commercial competition with IBM, DEC, Data General, Wang and Hewlett-Packard.

lead.headline: AT&T Throws Down a Unix Gauntlet With Six 3B Computers
lead.dek: The post-divestiture giant puts Unix System V and its own 32-bit architecture at the center of a sweeping commercial challenge.
body: AT&T formally entered the general-purpose computer business on March 27, opening a campaign that reaches from a desktop multi-user machine to fault-tolerant systems. Only months after the Bell System divestiture, the company is carrying Bell Labs software and AT&T-designed processors into direct competition with IBM, DEC, Data General, Wang and Hewlett-Packard.

Six announced models make up the 3B family, and every one runs AT&T Unix System V. The desktop 3B2 uses a 32-bit architecture, comes with 256K of memory and can serve as many as 18 users or work as a single-user machine. The larger 3B5 employs AT&T’s WE 32000 microprocessor, with versions intended for roughly 30 or 60 users.

At the upper end, the 3B20D emphasizes fault tolerance for banking, reservation and military work. AT&T says more than 1,200 related 3B20S systems are already operating inside its own companies, giving the sales pitch a substantial in-house proving ground.

The opening route is deliberately commercial: value-added resellers and customers able to provide applications come first, joined by 3B Net and a PC Interface. AT&T says 800 sales and technical people have been trained and plans a 6,000-person sales force by year’s end, while Olivetti handles European marketing.

The line’s first public showing is scheduled for COMDEX Winter in Los Angeles, April 5-7. Hardware sales are only part of the stakes: if the 3B family wins converts, Unix System V could move from a respected technical foundation toward the broad industry standard AT&T plainly wants it to become.

stories.headline: Police Raids Put Britain’s Games-Cassette Pirates Under Pressure
body: Police and Trading Standards raids reported in Salford and Hull have put unusually concrete numbers on the commercial counterfeiting trade. Ocean Software director David Ward estimated that a Salford warehouse held about 20,000 cassettes with a retail value near £100,000; police valued the blank media at £9,500.

Named copies included current games such as Jet Set Willy, Atic-Atac, Bugaboo and Harrier Attack. A separate Hull seizure recovered 150 cassettes after a tip from Software Projects. The actions target bulk sellers under deception and trade-description law, not home users, and charges in Hull had not yet been brought at press time.

stories.headline: IBM Rations PCs and XTs as the Component Squeeze Bites
body: IBM has limited dealers to 25 PC and XT machines a month and is quoting delivery four weeks after orders, a striking restriction for the market’s fastest-growing personal-computer standard. The shortage reaches Intel 8088 processors, 64K RAM chips and TTL components.

The squeeze lands only two weeks after IBM announced 20 percent price cuts. A licensing agreement with Intel and pilot U.S. production of the 8088 point toward relief, but for now dealers must ration machines just as lower prices promise to stimulate demand.

stories.headline: Sinclair Microdrives Reach London Shops
body: Forty long-awaited Sinclair Microdrives reached Computers of Wigmore Street, where six sold within half an hour. The miniature cartridge drive costs £49.95, or £79.95 with Interface 1; blank cartridges are £4.95.

Sinclair expects to send 20,000 Microdrive and Interface 1 units into shops each month. After delays severe enough to create a black market in order forms, an ordinary retail sale is news in itself, though full QL production is still taking time.

stories.headline: Macintosh Commands the West Coast Computer Faire
body: Apple gave away one Macintosh each day at the ninth West Coast Computer Faire in San Francisco, where the compact new machine drew the show’s liveliest attention. Elsewhere, IBM PC software dominated and exhibitors increasingly bundled “wordware” with programs.

The floor offered little major new hardware, but falling storage prices stood out: Electro Mavin advertised a 20MB eight-inch Winchester drive for the equivalent of about £1,100. A closing seminar on “The Personal Computing Backlash” captured an industry wondering what remains after the home-computer price war.

issues.editorNote: A bold graphics machine reaches for a place beyond strict IBM imitation, while games, accessibility and packaged software show just how many directions the microcomputer market is taking.
issues.morningLine: The Mindset PC gambles on color, speed and a distinctive visual identity.

lead.headline: Mindset PC Bets on Custom Color Graphics
lead.dek: An 80186, MS-DOS and purpose-built video hardware aim the new machine at artists, animators and game makers.
body: The newest challenge to the IBM-shaped personal-computer market arrives with a very different sales pitch: do more with the picture. InfoWorld placed the Mindset computer on its March 19 cover under the teasing line “Gambling on Great Graphics,” giving the ambitious machine one of the week’s most conspicuous introductions.

Inside is Intel’s 80186 processor and MS-DOS, but the headline attraction is custom graphics hardware rather than strict IBM compatibility. The system can display 320 by 200 pixels with 16 colors at once, a specification meant to make painting, animation and game work feel native instead of added as an afterthought.

Mindset Designer supplies the showcase. The paint program’s tools and colorful sample art turn the computer into a visual workstation, and contemporary documentation identifies programmer Kevin Furry and artist Whitney Caughlan among the people behind the package.

That specialty is also the wager. Buyers now have abundant software and familiar IBM-compatible choices, so a distinctive display must justify stepping away from the safest standard. Mindset is betting that a vivid screen and responsive graphics can create a market of their own.

stories.headline: Microcomputers Become Tools of Independence
body: The March 19 InfoWorld cover also points toward a quieter revolution: personal computers adapted for people with disabilities. Period rehabilitation research compared machines from Apple, Epson, IBM and others as aids for communication, environmental control and information access.

The work treats the micro not merely as office equipment but as a flexible interface. Alternate input devices and specialized software can turn a general-purpose home computer into a practical bridge to writing, learning and control of everyday surroundings.

stories.headline: Laserdiscs Point Toward an Arcade-Style Future at Home
body: Computer & Video Games is asking whether laserdiscs can bring the spectacle of the new arcade cabinets into the living room. Full-motion filmed imagery promises a visual leap far beyond sprites, even if cost, storage and interaction still make the route uncertain.

The same March issue previews Atari’s Major Havoc and Marvin’s Maze and reviews joysticks across micros and video systems. Together they show a games market testing new pictures and new controls while home computers and consoles increasingly share the same shelf.

stories.headline: Chequered Flag Takes the British Micro Pole
body: The RAM/C all-formats chart published March 17 puts Sinclair’s Chequered Flag at No. 1, ahead of Manic Miner and Fighter Pilot. Atic Atac and Scuba Dive complete a top five packed with fast, inexpensive microcomputer play.

The list captures the variety of the Spectrum-era shelf: motor racing, platform action, flight simulation, maze adventure and undersea exploration. Ultimate Play the Game also has Lunar Jetman and Jetpac farther down the chart, evidence of a vigorous specialist software trade.

issues.editorNote: The home-computer price war has claimed another famous name, even as ambitious graphics machines and a crowded software trade show point toward what comes next.
issues.morningLine: Timex leaves the Sinclair computer business while Softcon fills New Orleans with software, graphics and argument.

lead.headline: Timex Pulls the Plug on Its Sinclair Home Computers
lead.dek: The watchmaker joins Texas Instruments and Mattel in retreat, turning the post-boom home-computer shakeout into the week’s unmistakable story.
body: Timex will cease production and sales of its Timex/Sinclair 1500 and 2068 home computers, ending one of the most visible attempts to put a microcomputer into American homes at a mass-market price. The company says manufacturing will stop after remaining components are used, probably within four months.

Only a short time ago, the sub-$100 Timex/Sinclair 1000 commanded an estimated 28 percent of the home market. But aggressive competition from Commodore and Texas Instruments forced reductions on the later 1500 and 2068, while the collapse of the 1983 price war left retailers and manufacturers with painful inventories.

Timex marketing vice president C. Michael Jacobi calls the market “risky and volatile.” The withdrawal puts Timex beside Texas Instruments and Mattel among major consumer names backing away from home computers, and it raises a sober question for buyers: which inexpensive machine will still have software and service next year?

Sinclair insists its own business and planned $500 direct-mail launch of the 32-bit QL will continue. Timex’s Dundee plant is also expected to remain Sinclair’s largest contract manufacturer. The brand partnership may persist behind factory doors, but on American store shelves the Timex/Sinclair experiment is ending.

stories.headline: Mindset Bets Its PC Future on Spectacular Graphics
body: Former Atari computer chief Roger Badertscher is preparing an April launch for Mindset, a $1,099 80186-based machine built around custom graphics coprocessors. Its animation and color modes aim at a creative market that ordinary IBM compatibles barely address.

Storage sharply raises the bill: one floppy adds $699 and two drives add $1,299. Mindset says it tested 60 unmodified IBM PC programs, plans Microsoft Windows support and will offer the $399 Lumena graphics package. A $40 joystick makes the system’s game and animation ambitions plain.

stories.headline: VisiCalc Partners Carry Their Feud to Softcon
body: Software Arts, creator of VisiCalc, has announced its own Advanced Version for IBM PCs after moving to end its long marketing arrangement with VisiCorp. A Massachusetts court refused VisiCorp’s request to stop Software Arts from using the famous trademark.

Owners can obtain a promotional $99.95 upgrade, but the six months of suits and countersuits expose a new software-industry reality: a program name, its distribution rights and its installed audience can be as valuable as the code itself.

stories.headline: Model 100 Gains a Desktop-Sized Disk Drive
body: Radio Shack’s portable Model 100 can now connect to a $799, 5.25-inch disk unit, with room for a $240 second drive. Each single-sided floppy holds 184K in a format incompatible with other TRS-80 disks.

The enclosure is not portable, but it adds monitor and television connections and a 25-line display. For owners of a 16K or larger Model 100, the accessory turns a road machine into a more capable office system when it returns to the desk.

issues.editorNote: Software is no longer merely what comes in the box. This week it commands its own shows, export ambitions and a multibillion-dollar trade.
issues.morningLine: Software takes center stage while IBM’s junior PC meets the reviewers.

lead.headline: Software Steps Out of Hardware’s Shadow
lead.dek: A multibillion-dollar American trade looks overseas—and a software show makes clear that programs now constitute an industry of their own.
body: The personal-computer business has spent years measuring progress in processors, memory and disk drives. This week the programs themselves claim the marquee. A March 4 report in The Washington Post describes American personal-computer software as a multibillion-dollar business whose firms are looking beyond the domestic boom toward customers overseas.

Two days later, The New York Times filed “The View From a Software Show.” The timing matters: a gathering organized around programs rather than machines signals a trade gaining its own professional rhythm—publishers, dealers, demonstrations and buyers comparing what computers can actually do.

The opportunity comes with friction. Apple, IBM, Commodore, Atari and Britain’s flourishing micro makers divide the market among incompatible formats. Every successful title therefore brings choices about conversion, distribution and support, while buyers must ask whether the software shelf behind a machine is broad enough to justify its price.

Hardware still sets the limits, but software increasingly determines which machine earns desk space. The industry’s next contest will be fought not only over specifications, but over the programs that turn boxes of chips into useful—and entertaining—personal tools.

stories.headline: IBM’s PCjr Arrives to a Skeptical Reception
body: IBM’s home-minded PCjr reaches its retail-launch month carrying the family name, an 8088-class processor, cartridge slots, enhanced color graphics, three-voice sound and a wireless infrared keyboard. The entry configuration is quoted at $669 to $699, while the 128K enhanced model with a disk drive lists for $1,269 before a monitor.

Reviewers find the compromises as conspicuous as the features. Creative Computing examines limits in compatibility and expansion and sharply criticizes the small chiclet-style keyboard. BYTE’s March newsstand lineup also gives the junior machine close attention. IBM has entered the living room, but buyers must decide whether the badge compensates for the awkward keys and a fully equipped price well above the headline figure.

stories.headline: Micro Games Crowd the Chart
body: The RAM/C all-formats chart published by Personal Computer News on March 17 measures sales through March 8, placing it squarely inside this issue week. Chequered Flag leads, followed by Manic Miner, Fighter Pilot, Atic Atac and Scuba Dive—a top five dominated by the lively British home-computer trade.

That chart complicates the American tale of a videogame crash. Dedicated cartridge consoles may be suffering, yet software for programmable micros remains a vigorous retail business. Activision’s H.E.R.O. and FTL’s Sundog: Frozen Legacy also belong to the March 1984 release conversation, though surviving records do not support a precise street day this week.

stories.headline: Industry Seeks Laws Against “Electronic Trespassers”
body: The Videotex Industry Association is pressing state and federal lawmakers for measures against unauthorized computer access. Its claim that electronic trespass costs members millions of dollars each month is an industry estimate, not an independently audited total, but the appeal shows network intrusion moving into commercial and legislative debate.

A March issue of the young publication 2600 meanwhile gives the emerging hacker and phone-phreak culture a printed voice. Together the artifacts capture a widening argument over access, curiosity, property and law. The period sources supply no named crew behind the association’s complaint, and this account offers no access codes or operational instructions.

issues.morningLine: This week in 1984: IBM’s 30-pound portable arrives, the West Coast Computer Faire opens, and software takes center stage.

lead.headline: IBM Packs the PC Into a 30-Pound Portable
lead.dek: Big Blue answers the transportable-computer boom with a suitcase-sized machine that runs familiar PC software.
body: IBM announced the Portable Personal Computer 5155 Model 68 on February 29, bringing its own badge to a transportable category pioneered by Osborne and sharpened by Compaq. The new machine preserves IBM PC disk and software compatibility in a luggable case intended to move between desks.

Inside are an Intel 8088, 256K of memory, a nine-inch amber display and one 360K double-sided 5.25-inch diskette drive. The keyboard clips over the front for travel, while five expansion slots leave room for the familiar boards that have helped turn the PC into a business standard.

Portability remains a relative term. The 5155 weighs about 30 pounds, measures roughly 20 by 17 by 8 inches and requires an AC outlet. At $4,225 before a second drive or other options, it is built for professionals who value compatibility and mobility more than a light load.

The announcement confirms that transportable PCs are no passing novelty. IBM now expects customers to carry their software environment between offices, and rivals must answer a machine that combines the market leader’s name with the appeal of a computer that can travel.

stories.headline: West Coast Computer Faire Throws Open Its Doors
body: The ninth West Coast Computer Faire runs March 2-4 at San Francisco’s Civic Auditorium and Brooks Hall, gathering vendors, user groups and enthusiasts under one roof. Its show daily and proceedings range across software, floppy disks, communications and practical microcomputer applications.

The gathering remains part marketplace and part classroom. Timex/Sinclair clubs and other user communities stand beside commercial exhibitors, a reminder that personal computing is still being built jointly by manufacturers and people trading hard-won knowledge.

stories.headline: Software Becomes the Industry’s Main Event
body: Softcon in New Orleans drew a reported 14,600 visitors and 600 exhibitors to a show devoted entirely to software publishing. More than 12,000 packages were displayed as an industry once treated as an accessory to hardware asserted its own economic weight.

Industry estimates put 1984 software sales near $3.5 billion with growth of 40 to 50 percent a year. Lotus previewed Symphony, extending the 1-2-3 idea with fuller word processing, filing and communications, while publishers confronted development and launch costs that could reach millions.

stories.headline: PCjr Brings Better Games—and Awkward Compromises
body: IBM’s PCjr reaches reviewers with enhanced color graphics and sound, joystick support and instant-loading ROM cartridges. The $669 entry model carries 64K; the $1,269 enhanced version adds 128K and a 360K disk drive.

Its light system unit and gaming talents widen the PC family, but the infrared 62-key keyboard draws criticism and disk activity can swallow keystrokes. Reviewers see promise, yet cheaper dedicated game machines remain formidable rivals in the living room.

issues.editorNote: The IBM-compatible tide rises as Zenith enters the field, IBM presses its firmware claims, and PC software and accessories fill dealer pages.
issues.morningLine: Zenith joins the compatible rush while software, mice and modems crowd the personal-computer marketplace.

lead.headline: Zenith Joins the IBM-Compatible Rush With New 16-Bit PCs
lead.dek: The electronics veteran enters the hottest race in personal computing with a 16-bit family built to speak IBM’s language.
body: Zenith Data Systems unveiled its Z-150 family on February 22, placing another substantial manufacturer in the fast-growing market for machines compatible with the IBM Personal Computer. The new 16-bit line is aimed at buyers who want access to the expanding IBM software world without buying an IBM-badged machine.

Compatibility has become the industry’s most valuable promise. Businesses are accumulating programs, files and training around the PC standard, and every new entrant must convince customers that familiar software and peripherals will travel safely to its hardware. Zenith brings an established dealer and institutional presence to that contest.

The arrival also sharpens a difficult question: how closely may a rival follow IBM’s design? The week’s settlement between IBM and Eagle Computer over firmware copyright shows that software hidden inside the box can matter as much as the chips and disk drives advertised outside it.

For buyers, the result is a broader field and more pressure on prices. For manufacturers, it is a race to offer compatibility while retaining enough engineering independence to stay outside IBM’s legal sights.

stories.headline: IBM and Eagle Settle Firmware Copyright Fight
body: IBM and Eagle Computer settled their dispute over copyrighted firmware this week, adding a legal boundary marker to the compatible-computer boom. IBM has argued that copying the code that starts and controls a PC infringes its copyright even when a rival builds otherwise independent hardware.

The settlement warns clone makers that compatibility cannot simply mean reproducing IBM’s internal instructions. Manufacturers increasingly need independently written firmware—a clean route to the same behavior—if they want to sell access to PC software without inviting a courtroom fight.

stories.headline: Software Industry Comes Into Its Own
body: The personal-computer software trade is emerging as an industry in its own right, with applications, utilities and specialist publishers multiplying around popular machines. Dealer pages now present software as a shelf of competing products rather than an afterthought bundled with hardware.

Microsoft is pushing Word alongside its mouse, while database managers promise links to spreadsheets and word processors and small utilities such as Norton’s win space in the same crowded market. The value of a computer increasingly rests on what buyers can make it do after the box reaches the desk.

stories.headline: PC Magazine Pits Apple Experience Against IBM Momentum
body: PC Magazine’s February issue captures a market divided between Apple’s carefully designed user experience and the IBM PC’s gathering commercial momentum. Buyers are weighing graphical ease and integration against the immense tide of compatible hardware and software.

That contrast is shaping the next phase of personal computing. Apple asks users to adopt a distinct way of working; the IBM camp offers a widening bazaar of interchangeable pieces, dealer discounts and familiar business programs.

lead.headline: IBM Packs the PC into a 30-Pound Suitcase
lead.dek: The $4,225 Portable Personal Computer answers Compaq with PC/XT compatibility, twin floppy drives and a built-in amber screen.
body: IBM entered the suitcase-computer contest on February 16 with the Portable Personal Computer model 5155, putting the familiar IBM PC architecture into a transportable case. Contemporary coverage made the competitive target plain: Compaq had proved that business buyers wanted a machine they could carry between offices without leaving their software behind.

Inside, the new portable followed the PC/XT line with a 4.77 MHz Intel 8088 processor and 256 KB of memory, expandable to 640 KB. Two 360 KB 5.25-inch floppy drives sat beside a built-in 9-inch amber display, while the detachable keyboard clipped across the front for travel.

Portable remained a relative term. The 5155 weighed about 30 pounds, required AC power and cost $4,225. It was a luggable business computer rather than a battery-powered laptop, aimed at professionals who valued IBM compatibility enough to carry the weight and pay the premium.

That compatibility may be the machine’s strongest feature. Buyers could take established IBM PC programs and disks on the road, and corporate departments could add a mobile system without adopting a separate software standard. The 5155 shows how quickly the compatible-PC market is forcing IBM to answer categories created by its rivals.

stories.headline: Sinclair Sets a $499 American Course for the QL
body: Sinclair Research said on February 13 that it planned to bring the QL to American consumers in the fall for $499. The Quantum Leap uses a Motorola 68008 processor, carries 128 KB of memory and aims above Sinclair’s inexpensive ZX home machines at home-office and small-business users.

Its value pitch is unusually ambitious: two built-in Microdrives, a professional keyboard, color-display capability and a bundled Psion suite covering word processing, spreadsheets, databases and business graphics. The promised price puts pressure on machines costing several times more, though American buyers must wait to see whether Sinclair meets its delivery plans.

stories.headline: CBS, IBM and Sears Bet on a Videotex Home
body: CBS, IBM and Sears joined forces in the electronic information-services field this week, combining a broadcaster, the dominant computer maker and a retail giant in a bid to reach consumers by telephone line. The alliance intensifies the race to turn home terminals into gateways for news, shopping, banking and communications.

The venture reflects a sweeping expectation that networked information will become a household business. Modems remain slow and the audience small, but the partners bring content, technical reach and retail familiarity to a market still searching for the service that will persuade families to go online.

stories.headline: Coleco Courts Publishers for Adam “Best Of” Albums
body: A tightly dated Electronic Games Hotline report says Coleco plans “best of” software albums for the Adam, seeking deals with established publishers to strengthen the computer’s thin catalog. The move follows a difficult holiday introduction marked by questions about reliability and performance.

Compilations could give Adam owners recognizable games while helping Coleco show that its computer has a future beyond bundled software. For now the report describes a publishing plan, not finished albums on store shelves; execution will matter as much as the names Coleco signs.

issues.editorNote: The personal-computer market is no longer merely choosing machines; it is choosing standards. This week, IBM compatibility becomes the question hanging over every desk, while Coleco works to rescue Adam with restarted production and a promised library of familiar games.
issues.morningLine: Good morning from 1984: the clones are gathering, Adam is back on the line, and Punch-Out!! is ringing the arcade bell.

lead.headline: IBM Compatibility Becomes the Industry’s New Battleground
lead.dek: An open hardware architecture, protected firmware and a vast software library turn “compatible” into the most valuable—and confusing—word in personal computing.
body: The flood of machines claiming kinship with the IBM Personal Computer has made compatibility one of the microcomputer trade’s most important and confusing questions. IBM published enough of the PC’s hardware design to invite expansion cards and outside development, but the machine’s basic input-output system remains copyrighted software. A look-alike case and an 8088-family processor alone do not make a true substitute.

For buyers, the test is practical. Will the machine boot the same operating system, run the same application programs, accept the same expansion cards and talk to the same printers and disks? Each “yes” gives a newcomer access to the broad catalog forming around the IBM standard. Each exception can turn a bargain into an island.

Clone builders therefore compete on more than price. Some promise portability, faster operation or more generous standard equipment; all must decide how closely to follow IBM without copying protected ROM code. Independently written firmware is becoming both an engineering achievement and a legal shield.

The result is a market reorganizing around software rather than badges. IBM created the reference machine, but a widening circle of compatible makers now wants the applications, dealers and customer confidence that surround it. The winner may be less a single computer than a common platform—provided shoppers learn exactly what each claim of compatibility means.

stories.headline: Coleco Restarts Adam Lines After a Gentleman’s C
body: Coleco resumed full Adam production at two upstate New York plants this week after a January inventory pause, returning its ambitious home computer to the line just as a prominent review assigned the machine an “A for ingenuity” but only a gentleman’s C for performance.

The roughly $600 package remains striking: a Z80A-based computer, keyboard, Digital Data Pack storage, daisy-wheel printer and ColecoVision cartridge compatibility in one box. Yet delayed deliveries and early reliability complaints have made dependable performance more urgent than the long feature list.

Restarting the factories can refill dealer shelves. Restoring confidence will require machines that work consistently—and enough worthwhile software to persuade families that Adam is more than a console with office ambitions.

stories.headline: “Best Of” Game Albums Promised for Adam
body: Coleco is courting established software publishers for “Best Of” collections intended to give Adam a faster route to a credible game catalog. Electronic Games Hotline led its February 12 issue with the plan, suggesting familiar titles could be assembled for the new machine rather than waiting for an entirely home-grown library.

The move recognizes the hard lesson of every new platform: specifications do not sell a computer for long without programs. Proven games could link Adam’s ColecoVision audience to its keyboard-and-printer future while buying developers time to create original software.

stories.headline: One Printer Attempts Double Duty
body: A new American printer reviewed this week tackles a familiar home-office compromise. Daisy-wheel machines make typewriter-crisp letters but offer little graphic freedom; dot-matrix printers draw charts and illustrations but often leave correspondence looking unmistakably computerized.

The attempt to bridge those jobs shows why the printer can be the most consequential accessory in a home system. A computer that calculates, writes and draws still needs one machine able to put all three kinds of work convincingly on paper.

milestone.title: Macintosh reaches the public
milestone.note: Steve Jobs’s January 30 Boston Computer Society presentation put the mouse-driven graphical computer before the world’s largest personal-computer user organization.

issues.editorNote: Six days after its unveiling, Macintosh meets an experienced public audience; elsewhere, IBM draws a hard legal line around the code inside PC compatibility.
issues.morningLine: The mouse takes the stage in Boston while the clone business heads for court.

lead.headline: Macintosh Meets the Public in Boston
lead.dek: Steve Jobs brings Apple’s new graphical computer before the Boston Computer Society for its first public demonstration.
body: BOSTON, Jan. 30 — Six days after Apple formally introduced Macintosh, Steve Jobs carried the compact computer onto the Boston Computer Society stage for what the society’s founder remembers as its first public showing. Before a room of experienced personal-computer users, the machine’s windows, icons and mouse moved from advertising promise to a working demonstration.

Jobs showed point-and-click commands, cutting and pasting between applications, mixed text and pictures, drawing tools, stacked desktop documents and even three-dimensional chess. The sequence made Apple’s central argument visible: ordinary work could be directed through consistent pictures and menus instead of a memorized command language.

The $2,495 launch model combines 128 kilobytes of RAM, 64 kilobytes of ROM, a built-in high-resolution monochrome display, a mouse and a 3.5-inch disk drive. Apple is including MacWrite and MacPaint for purchasers during the first 100 days, giving buyers immediate demonstrations of proportional type, page composition and bitmap drawing.

Microsoft Multiplan is available at launch, while Apple says more than 100 outside companies are developing products. The company also says its Fremont line can turn out one Macintosh every 27 seconds, but expects demand to outrun supply for several months.

The Boston appearance supplies the crucial test missing from launch-day spectacle: how the system behaves in front of knowledgeable users. Macintosh is still a costly, memory-tight first model, but its public debut makes the graphical desktop a concrete personal-computing proposition.

stories.headline: IBM Takes the Clone War to Court
body: IBM has sued makers of PC-compatible products over copyrighted code, putting the industry on notice that an open hardware bus does not make the PC’s basic input-output system free to copy. The ROM software at issue is what lets compatible hardware behave like an IBM machine.

The pressure separates functional compatibility from literal duplication. Vendors that want to share the IBM PC software market will need independently written BIOS code—a legal and engineering path that promises to shape which clone makers survive.

stories.headline: Lisa 2 Becomes Macintosh’s Elder Sibling
body: Apple has introduced three Lisa 2 models alongside Macintosh, describing the systems as one 32-bit graphical family. The revised Lisa line adopts the smaller 3.5-inch disk format and is intended to share software with the less expensive Macintosh.

The pairing gives Apple a ladder from the $2,495 compact desktop to higher-end office machines. February’s BYTE puts Macintosh on its cover while also examining Lisa 2, capturing Apple’s attempt to turn a new interface into a product family.

stories.headline: MacWrite and MacPaint Make the Desktop Tangible
body: MacWrite handles multiple fonts and sizes, search and replace, and pictures pasted into documents. MacPaint supplies brushes, pencils, erasers, textures and geometric shapes for bitmap illustration.

Bundling both programs during the first 100 days is more than a promotion: the pair demonstrates shared menus, cut and paste, proportional type and mixed graphics immediately after the box is opened. Microsoft Multiplan adds a familiar business application to the launch shelf.

stories.headline: Computer Games Ask What Comes After the Crash
body: February’s COMPUTE! asks both “What Makes A Good Game?” and “The Future Of Electronic Games” as the American cartridge-console trade contracts. The magazine’s machine-spanning coverage suggests that inventive play is migrating toward programmable home computers.

Its review of Computer War for Atari, VIC-20 and TI machines places nuclear strategy in the post-WarGames wave. The evidence is a monthly trend rather than a precise release diary, but it shows designers and players looking beyond arcade imitation toward deeper simulations.

milestone.title: Apple launches the Macintosh
milestone.note: The January 24 debut put a mass-market graphical desktop, icons, windows, mouse control, and consistent application design at the center of personal computing's future.

issues.editorNote: Extra Edition: Apple has placed the mouse, windows and pictures at the center of a $2,495 personal computer—and challenged the rest of the industry to follow.
issues.morningLine: Cupertino opens a new window on personal computing while Atari regroups and home-computer shelves keep moving.

lead.headline: Macintosh Arrives: Apple Bets $2,495 on the Mouse
lead.dek: The compact 128K machine brings Lisa-style windows, icons and graphics to a far wider market—and seeks a place beside the Apple II and IBM PC.
body: CUPERTINO, Calif.—Apple Computer unveiled the Macintosh on January 24, placing a mouse-controlled graphical desktop inside a compact 20-pound machine carrying a suggested retail price of $2,495. Apple chairman Steven P. Jobs declared that the company expected Macintosh to become a third industry standard alongside the Apple II and IBM PC.

The specifications make the wager concrete: 128KB of memory, 64KB of read-only memory, a crisp black-and-white screen, one 3.5-inch disk drive, two serial ports, an external-drive connection and built-in sound. Menus, icons and overlapping windows replace much command-line ritual, while cut and paste lets words and pictures travel between documents.

For its first 100 days, Macintosh buyers receive MacWrite and MacPaint without extra charge. MacWrite mixes typefaces, sizes and illustrations; MacPaint supplies brushes, patterns, shapes and erasers. Microsoft Multiplan is available immediately, Lotus has promised a Macintosh version of 1-2-3, and Apple says more than 100 outside companies are developing products.

The polish comes with limits. Macintosh runs one major application at a time, and a contemporary test found that changing programs to move a picture into a letter could take 20 to 30 seconds. Its 128K memory and single internal drive leave little room to spare, even as the interface makes the computer feel unusually approachable.

Apple is backing the launch with a $15 million, 100-day advertising drive following Ridley Scott's nationally aired “1984” commercial during the January 22 Super Bowl. A Fremont factory is prepared to turn out one Macintosh every 27 seconds; now dealers, universities, offices and home users will decide whether Apple's new desktop language becomes computing's next vernacular.

stories.headline: Lisa 2 Family Cuts the Price of Apple’s Workstation
body: Apple also introduced three Lisa 2 configurations priced from roughly $3,500 to $5,500—far below the original Lisa's near-$10,000 ticket. The machines offer more storage and power than Macintosh and can keep several applications running at once.

The shared 3.5-inch disk format and planned software connections make Lisa 2 the senior member of a family rather than a solitary executive machine. Jobs conceded that the first Lisa suffered from high price, thin software support and an overly narrow Fortune 500 sales focus.

stories.headline: MacWrite and MacPaint Lead the Software Parade
body: Apple's two bundled programs are more than demonstrations: they define the new machine's point-and-click vocabulary. MacWrite combines varied fonts with search, replacement and pasted illustrations; MacPaint turns the mouse into a pencil, brush, eraser and geometric drafting tool.

Apple expects independent publishers to supply about 90 percent of Macintosh software and forecasts at least 500 packages by year's end. Microsoft, Lotus and Software Publishing Corporation are among the named supporters, while Apple's coming MacTerminal is meant to connect the compact machine to larger systems.

stories.headline: Atari Reorders the Front Office as the Game Crash Bites
body: Atari realigned management on January 24 as James Morgan continued the difficult work of stabilizing Warner Communications' battered games subsidiary. The change follows steep 1983 reversals and extensive layoffs amid the contraction of the American console market.

The home-computer side remains active despite the corporate strain. Period catalogs show games, disk drives, printer gear and utilities still arriving for the Atari 400/800 and XL audience—a busy shelf beneath a company fighting to restore order above it.

stories.headline: Satellite Television Aims Straight at the Home
body: The nation's first direct-to-home satellite television service is preparing to begin operation, UPI reported January 25. The plan promises pictures delivered from orbit without depending on a local broadcaster or a neighborhood cable plant.

Receiving equipment and economics will determine how broadly the experiment travels, but the debut marks home satellite reception as one of consumer electronics' most forward-looking distribution bets.

milestone.title: Apple's '1984' commercial introduces Macintosh to a national audience
milestone.note: The Super Bowl broadcast made the graphical, mouse-driven Macintosh a mass-market cultural event and a landmark in computing and advertising history.

issues.editorNote: Extra edition: one extraordinary minute of television turns a forthcoming personal computer into a national conversation.
issues.morningLine: Macintosh steps from the trade press onto America’s biggest screen.

lead.headline: APPLE'S ‘1984’ SPOT PUTS MACINTOSH ON THE NATIONAL STAGE
lead.dek: A stark Super Bowl film promises a new kind of personal computer before viewers have even seen the machine itself.
body: During Super Bowl XVIII on January 22, Apple Computer used a single dramatic national broadcast to introduce the Macintosh as more than another machine. Ridley Scott’s film showed gray ranks of workers facing a giant screen until a lone runner smashed it, closing with Apple’s promise that 1984 would not resemble George Orwell’s 1984.

The commercial offered scarcely a conventional product demonstration. Its target was an idea: personal computing as an escape from conformity. That approach put the still-unreleased Macintosh before a mass audience with a cultural vocabulary far removed from memory counts and expansion slots.

Apple’s product plans supplied the substance behind the spectacle. Reports during the week described Macintosh as part of a broader 32-bit line alongside revised Lisa models, while Apple’s launch material emphasized a graphical display, mouse control, MacWrite and MacPaint at a suggested retail price of $2,495.

The advertisement’s reach made the Macintosh launch a public event before the January 24 unveiling. For the personal-computer business, the week marked a shift: machines would now be sold not only by specifications and price, but by an image of who their owners hoped to become.

stories.headline: APPLE READIES A 32-BIT FAMILY AROUND MACINTOSH AND LISA 2
body: Apple’s January plans linked the compact Macintosh to revised Lisa systems, placing the company’s graphical interface and mouse-driven approach across a broader product family.

MacWrite and MacPaint showed how fonts, cut-and-paste editing and bitmap drawing could make the interface tangible to ordinary users. The $2,495 suggested Macintosh price still put that experience well above bargain home computers.

stories.headline: COMMODORE 264 BETS ON SOFTWARE BUILT INTO THE MACHINE
body: At Winter CES, Commodore’s 264 and talking 364V prototypes pointed beyond the VIC-20 and Commodore 64. Their 3-PLUS-1 package placed word processing, files, spreadsheets and graphics in ROM.

The new family sacrificed direct Commodore 64 software compatibility, a consequential gamble when the C64 library was becoming one of the company’s strongest advantages. Pricing remained unsettled, leaving buyers to weigh convenience against continuity.

stories.headline: COLECO PROMISES A LARGER ADAM WORLD AMID QUALITY QUESTIONS
body: Coleco arrived at CES promising more peripherals and software for Adam, seeking to turn the all-in-one computer into an expanding home system.
But reports of defective early units continued to shadow the pitch. Dealers quoted roughly $700 to $799 in New York, making reliability as important as the machine’s ambitious bundle.

milestone.title: Jack Tramiel abruptly leaves Commodore
milestone.note: The departure ended the leadership era that made the VIC-20 and Commodore 64 mass-market machines and would soon reshape both Commodore and Atari.

issues.editorNote: EXTRA: Commodore’s founder departs just as the home-computer price war reaches a decisive turn.
issues.morningLine: The billion-dollar home-computer giant awakens without the man who built its low-price empire.

lead.headline: TRAMIEL QUITS COMMODORE
lead.dek: Founder’s surprise Friday resignation, days after his CES appearance, leaves the company’s next generation under a cloud.
body: Jack Tramiel resigned as president and chief executive of Commodore International on Friday, January 13, an abrupt break at the company he had driven from office-machine roots into the center of the home-computer boom. The news followed only days after Tramiel personally championed Commodore’s new 264 family at the Winter Consumer Electronics Show.

The timing makes the departure more than an executive shuffle. Commodore’s VIC-20 and Commodore 64 had turned price into a weapon, putting capable color computers into mass-market stores and forcing every rival to answer. COMPUTE! estimated that the company’s annual sales pace had multiplied roughly twenty-fivefold in six or seven years.

Tramiel said a billion-dollar company now required a “professional executive.” Marshall F. Smith, an industrial executive with manufacturing and finance experience but no computer-industry background, was expected to take charge in late February. Until then, dealers and developers must judge whether Commodore’s famously aggressive course will continue.

The unanswered question hangs over the 264 and speech-equipped 364V. Both promise 64K, an improved BASIC and built-in productivity tools, but sacrifice much of the Commodore 64’s game compatibility. The machines arrived as the industry’s shakeout became visible; now their most forceful sponsor has left the stage.

stories.headline: Games Trade Finds Guarded Relief at CES
body: After the bruising 1983 market collapse, the New York Times found a “sigh of relief” among video-game exhibitors on January 10. The confidence was cautious: companies were narrowing their lines, emphasizing proven machines and searching for ways to keep cartridge buyers interested.

Mattel Electronics had been sold to investors, yet its booth still showed a System Changer for Atari 2600 cartridges, new Intellivision games and Apple and IBM titles. Computer Entertainer’s January tally kept Miner 2049er, Ms. Pac-Man and River Raid among the period’s strongest sellers.

The show-floor message is survival through software and compatibility. The arcade spirit remains alive, but the extravagant hardware race has yielded to sharper bets on games people will actually buy.

stories.headline: Commodore’s 264 Family Promises an Office in ROM
body: The 264 and talking 364V pair 64K of memory with BASIC 3.5, whose disk, graphics, sound and structured-programming commands answer long-standing complaints about the Commodore 64’s sparse built-in language. More than 59K is available to BASIC.

Commodore’s proposed 3-Plus-1 package combines word processing, filing, spreadsheet work and business graphics. The 364V adds a numeric keypad and Magic Voice speech synthesis, aiming squarely at buyers who want an appliance rather than a hobby kit.

That convenience carries a cost: C64 cartridges, joysticks and Datasette gear do not transfer, and the TED chip lacks the C64’s sprites and celebrated SID sound. Commodore says the 264 will sell below $500, but has announced no firm price.

stories.headline: Coleco Builds an Adam Comeback Plan
body: Coleco answered Adam’s troubled debut with a large CES expansion plan: a floppy drive, modem, RAM card, second data drive, CP/M support and a pledge of 170 software packages. Honeywell had opened five service centers and planned thirty more.

Questions remain over reliability and price. Creative Computing cited published claims of high initial defect rates, which a Coleco spokesman rejected, while wholesale pricing rose about 20 percent to $650 and New York retail quotes reached $700 to $799.
The accessories could turn Adam into a broader computer system, but the comeback now depends on delivery, service and restoring buyer confidence.
