milestone.title: Amiga Lorraine's first press demonstration
milestone.note: The secret Winter CES prototype previewed the custom-chip multimedia architecture that would define the Amiga and influence graphics, sound and gaming computers for years.

issues.editorNote: Extra Edition: Winter CES opens a decisive year with new Commodore machines and a private glimpse of Amiga’s next-generation Lorraine prototype.
issues.morningLine: LAS VEGAS — A crowded Commodore stand and a secret Amiga demonstration set the pace as the home-computer business enters its shakeout year.

lead.headline: Commodore's 264 family steals a shakeout-era Winter CES
lead.dek: Commodore draws the Winter CES crowds with two 64K machines, built-in productivity software and a new BASIC—while leaving price and compatibility questions open.
body: The International Winter Consumer Electronics Show opened in Las Vegas on January 7 and ran through January 10; COMPUTE! estimated attendance at 80,000-90,000 and said the Commodore stand was crowded throughout the show. Commodore announced the 264 and speech-equipped 364V, both with 64K RAM and a 7501-family processor running at about 1.76 MHz.

The machines used the TED chip, offered 16 colors at eight luminance levels (128 shades), but omitted the Commodore 64's sprites and sophisticated SID-style three-voice sound, providing two simpler tone generators instead. BASIC 3.5 added structured-programming, graphics, sound, disk, error-trapping and editing commands; more than 59K was available to BASIC versus about 38K on the Commodore 64.

Buyers were to choose built-in ROM software such as Superscript, EasyCalc, 3-Plus-1, Logo, PILOT or Magic Desk II; the 364V added a numeric keypad and speech synthesis. No firm price was announced. Commodore told COMPUTE! the 264 would retail below $500 and the 364V slightly higher; Creative Computing reported industry guesses near $300 and below $500 respectively.

Compatibility was mixed: 1541 serial drives and some user-port devices would work, but old Datasette units, joysticks and Commodore 64 cartridges would not because connectors and the cartridge port changed. COMPUTE! described this CES as the start of the long-predicted home-computer shakeout: Atari had canceled the 1400XL, IBM stayed away after showing PCjr at COMDEX, and Texas Instruments displayed no TI-99/4A after quitting the market.

stories.headline: Behind a secret CES door, Amiga shows 'Lorraine'
body: Creative Computing editor John J. Anderson saw Lorraine privately at Winter CES; it was absent from Amiga's public booth and still built from breadboards, with production custom chips expected in April or May. Amiga president Dave Morse said sales of the company's Joyboard and other accessories had helped bankroll the computer project.

The custom VLSI chipset was designed by Jay Miner, designer of the original Atari computer chipset. The prototype delivered multicolor real-time animation, sprites, NTSC and RGB output, and four-voice stereo sound intended to feed a home sound system.

The planned machine had 128K RAM, a high-density 5.25-inch disk drive and a ROM cartridge slot; Anderson inferred a 68000-class processor but Morse did not confirm it. Amiga said it would cost less than a fully configured IBM PCjr; IBM compatibility was contemplated through an add-on processor cartridge.

stories.headline: Home-computer boom gives way to a fight for survival
body: COMPUTE! found far fewer new home computers than at the previous summer show, when 17 new machines had appeared. Atari showed its XL line but had officially canceled the 1400XL and offered only vague statements on the 1450XLD.

Spectravideo dropped the SV-318 in favor of an upgraded SV-328 Mark II and the SVI-728 MSX. Spectravideo's booth demonstration mocked Coleco's Adam by sawing one in half and dropping it into a trash can while a flushing sound played; Coleco representative Barbara Wruck said show management had forced removal of a real toilet used on the first day.
Apple attended but held Macintosh for its stockholders meeting later in January; IBM did not attend, having shown PCjr at COMDEX.

stories.headline: Kodak jumps into home video with a one-piece 8mm camcorder
body: Eastman Kodak unveiled its one-piece 8mm color camera-recorder system in New York on January 4, entering the home-video market. Contemporary reports emphasized that the unit combined camera and recorder rather than requiring a separate deck.

RCA simultaneously unveiled a 2.2-pound palm-sized color video camera but predicted 8mm consumer adoption would wait until 1985 or 1986. The Kodak announcement came immediately before Winter CES and represented a direct challenge to established VHS and Betamax equipment.

issues.editorNote: The final week of 1983 puts IBM’s long-awaited home computer under a reviewer’s lamp while Apple and Microsoft press graphical machines toward the office.
issues.morningLine: Junior arrives for inspection as the home-computer price war closes out a turbulent year.

lead.headline: The Little IBM Finally Arrives for Its Test
lead.dek: PCjr leaves the brochure and meets the reviewer, with color, sound, PC DOS—and a long list of extras.
body: IBM’s bid for the family room finally moved from announcement-stage promise to hands-on judgment this week. In a December 27 test, the New York Times examined the PCjr as a real machine rather than a specification sheet, asking whether the most famous name in business computing could translate its success to the home.

Junior keeps close to the IBM PC family with an Intel 8088-class processor and PC DOS, but adds enhanced color and sound for games, education, and household software. IBM’s brochure calls it “The easy one for everyone,” an appeal that places entertainment and schoolwork alongside writing, spreadsheets, and communications.

The entry model combines 64K with cassette storage for $669. A 128K machine with a disk drive lists at $1,269, before a monitor and many practical accessories. That makes the sticker price only the opening calculation for a household comparing Junior with sharply discounted Commodore and Atari machines.

The infrared Freeboard keyboard removes the cord but gives the machine one of its most conspicuous departures from the office PC. Its compact keys and the system’s constrained expansion scheme are likely to matter as much as the bright graphics when buyers decide whether IBM compatibility is worth the compromise.

PCjr therefore reaches stores carrying two burdens: it must feel friendly enough for first-time owners and compatible enough to borrow the IBM PC’s authority. The holiday test is over for 1983, but the market test has only begun.

stories.headline: Lisa Opens a Line to IBM and DEC
body: Apple is giving the Lisa a way into computer rooms already dominated by larger systems. LisaTerminal can emulate DEC VT100 and VT52 terminals as well as IBM 3278 terminals, UPI reported Wednesday.

Together with Apple’s Cluster Controller, the software lets Lisa users reach information and applications on IBM hosts and DEC minicomputers. The move answers a practical corporate objection to the costly graphical workstation: a new desktop cannot remain an island.

stories.headline: Christmas Computer Boom Leaves a Price-War Hangover
body: The year ends with home computers more visible—and less expensive—than ever. COMPUTE! found Commodore 64 street prices below $200 and VIC-20 machines below $100 as manufacturers fought for mass-market volume.

The bargains came with bruises. Commodore shortages affected computers and disk drives, Coleco’s delayed Adam lost precious holiday time, and retailers faced returns as newcomers discovered that a complete working system often required more than the box under the tree.

Future Computing estimated monthly shipments of 160,000 machines for Commodore, 100,000 for Texas Instruments, 65,000 for Atari, and 35,000 for Radio Shack. The shake-out has enlarged the audience while making survival harder for the companies supplying it.

stories.headline: Windows Proposes One Face for DOS Programs
stories.confidence: Same-month BYTE coverage of a pre-release system.
body: Microsoft’s proposed Windows environment offers tiled program windows, common menus, device handling, and mouse control above the growing base of MS-DOS machines. BYTE’s December coverage gives readers an early look at software meant to make unlike programs behave more consistently.

The system is still a promise rather than a store-shelf product, with Microsoft projecting availability in 1984. It joins Visi On and other graphical environments in a contest to decide whether the next PC interface will be learned by typing commands or pointing at choices.

stories.headline: Atari Finds a Holiday Bright Spot
body: Electronic Games Hotline’s final pre-Christmas issue reported a welcome boom in Atari hardware and software sales. The note offers a useful view from the shop floor during a year more often defined by excess inventory and corporate retrenchment.

One strong holiday report cannot settle the industry’s problems, but cartridges and computer games still command attention. Ultima III, Lode Runner, and M.U.L.E. show how ambitious disk software is broadening play beyond the familiar console formula.

issues.editorNote: IBM’s two-year-old personal computer now casts the industry’s longest shadow, while home-machine makers regroup for Christmas.
issues.morningLine: Big Blue defines the PC standard, Radio Shack refreshes the Color Computer, and holiday buyers hunt scarce drives and machines.

lead.headline: Big Blue Paints the Personal-Computer Standard
lead.dek: IBM captures the business desktop as software houses and add-on makers rally around its open specifications.
body: Only two years after entering personal computers, IBM has seized roughly 40 percent of the $2,000-to-$5,000 desktop market. That share tells only part of the story: the IBM PC has become the reference point against which business buyers, software publishers and would-be compatible makers now measure their plans.

More than 900 of the roughly 1,200 software companies operating before the PC appeared are now writing for IBM’s machine, according to this week’s industry assessment. New PC packages are arriving at a pace of about 50 each month, turning compatibility into a powerful sales argument for offices that want a broad catalog rather than a solitary machine.

IBM helped create that surrounding market by publishing technical specifications that independent manufacturers could study. Expansion boards, peripherals and compatible systems have multiplied, making the PC less a sealed product than the center of an increasingly busy commercial ecosystem.

The momentum also raises the stakes for every rival. Apple retains a devoted base and home computers compete fiercely below $1,000, but business software is gathering around Big Blue. At Christmas 1983, the most important feature of IBM’s PC may be the standard forming beyond the blue badge.

stories.headline: Home-Computer Price War Eases After a Savage 1983
body: The holiday market is emerging from a price war that pushed Texas Instruments out of home computers and left Atari nursing heavy losses. Commodore 64 street prices below $200 and VIC-20 prices below $100 delighted buyers, but the cuts punished manufacturers and dealers alike.

IBM’s PCjr, priced from roughly $700 to $1,300, has given surviving makers room to stop racing toward the bottom. Atari and Coleco raised prices after its unveiling, while shortages of components and popular disk drives put a practical floor beneath further holiday markdowns.

stories.headline: Radio Shack Refreshes the Color Computer Line
body: Radio Shack is answering the crowded holiday shelves with a 64K Extended BASIC Color Computer at $399.95 and two Color Computer 2 models at $239.95 and $319.95. All arrive with full-stroke keyboards, a welcome upgrade for buyers who intend to type more than game commands.

The 64K model can use its full memory with the $399.95 Color 2 Disk Kit and $69.95 OS-9 operating system, and can support as many as four drives. The less expensive Color Computer 2 machines retain cassette storage, keeping a lower-priced door open for first-time owners.

stories.headline: Lotus 1-2-3 Overtakes the Spreadsheet Pioneer
body: Lotus 1-2-3 is rapidly displacing VisiCalc as the business spreadsheet of choice. Its $495 package combines calculation, graphics and limited filing and writing tools, offering office buyers a coordinated suite rather than a single electronic ledger.

VisiCalc, once $350, has fallen to $250, but software prices remain tied to the costly work of development and support. Contemporary estimates place development of a major new program between $200,000 and $500,000, explaining why the strongest business titles resist the hardware market’s price war.

stories.headline: Christmas Computer Boom Meets Empty Shelves
body: The promised “Christmas of the Computer” has arrived unevenly. Commodore was shipping at enormous volume, yet Commodore 64 machines and disk drives could still be scarce, while Coleco’s Adam missed its August debut and reached FCC approval only in October.

Atari’s 600XL and 800XL were expected for Christmas, but delayed machines and canceled dealer orders made selection depend as much on availability as specifications. Families shopping this week may find that the computer in the advertisement is not the computer on the counter.

issues.editorNote: Extra Edition: the graphical desktop has become a shipping IBM PC product, even as rival window systems line up for 1984.
issues.morningLine: Visi On reaches the IBM PC, Nintendo sends Donkey Kong Jr. to arithmetic class, and the home-computer price war begins to cool.

lead.headline: The Window Wars Reach the IBM PC
lead.dek: Visi On ships a commercial graphical desktop while Microsoft and Quarterdeck ready cheaper rivals.
body: VisiCorp has put a windowed, mouse-driven working environment onto the IBM Personal Computer, turning a laboratory-style graphical interface into a commercial product. Visi On joins word processing, spreadsheet and graphing programs behind one visual system, giving business users a consistent way to move among tasks.

The elegance comes with demanding requirements. Applications must be written especially for Visi On, and the development system requires a costly minicomputer toolchain. Serious windowing also calls for roughly half a megabyte of memory and a hard disk, pushing a complete installation toward the expensive end of the PC market.

Microsoft is promising a different bargain for mid-1984. Its proposed Windows extension, projected at $100 to $250, uses tiled rather than overlapping windows and aims to standardize how programs address displays across machines. Microsoft president William Gates describes a neat-desk metaphor, a deliberate contrast with overlapping papers.

Quarterdeck’s DESQ, due in January, offers a third route: windows around most existing text-mode DOS applications without rewriting them. Graphics programs would still take over the full screen, but compatibility could matter more than visual polish to owners with established software libraries.

The contest is bigger than window decoration. Each company is bidding to control the common language between users, applications and displays. As analyst Egil Juliussen puts it, 1984 may determine who becomes the “window master of the world.”

stories.headline: Home-Computer Price War Finally Cools
body: After a year of punishing markdowns, manufacturers at COMDEX expect the steep slide in computer prices to moderate. Machines had been falling 20 to 25 percent annually, with even sharper cuts below $1,000; Texas Instruments has now quit the home-computer field and Atari has accumulated heavy losses.

IBM’s $700-to-$1,300 PCjr gives rivals room to retreat from the bottom. Atari and Coleco raised prices after its unveiling, while shortages of common PC components leave clone makers with little reason to discount. Kaypro president David Kay dissents, arguing that Japanese vendors may still move into the gap beneath PCjr.

stories.headline: Donkey Kong Jr. Clambers Into Arithmetic
body: Nintendo released Donkey Kong Jr. Math for the Family Computer in Japan on December 12. The ¥4,500 cartridge turns the familiar vine-climbing action into addition, subtraction, multiplication and division exercises, asking players to collect numbers and symbols.
Developed by Nintendo R&D1, it follows November’s Popeye English-learning title and shows how console makers hope recognizable arcade characters can broaden the family market beyond action games.

stories.headline: A Christmas Bounce for Atari Amid the Crash
body: Electronic Games Hotline led its December 18 number with an upbeat report that Atari hardware and software sales were booming for Christmas. The headline offers a rare bright patch in a year defined by excess cartridges, retailer caution and company losses.

The holiday lift does not erase the industry’s damage: Mattel has just reported a large quarterly loss and Atari’s computer division remains under pressure. But it suggests strong brands and attractive seasonal pricing can still move machines and games even in a contracting market.

stories.headline: Software Moves from Boxes to Parcels
body: Publishers are experimenting with splitting programs into modules and bundling related applications as software grows more costly to develop. Peachtree and Information Unlimited Software offer packages at roughly half the total price of their separate components.

Price itself has become a marketing signal. Business Systems raised an Apple II integrated package from $79 to $179 after deciding buyers equated cheap software with weak software, while Lotus 1-2-3 holds at $495 and VisiCalc has fallen to $250.

issues.editorNote: COMDEX has grown from a dealer gathering into an industry city, and nearly every aisle now bends toward the IBM PC. Beyond Las Vegas, floppy-disk fiction and fiercely priced home computers are making the holiday shelf every bit as consequential as the trade-show floor.
issues.morningLine: IBM compatibility commands COMDEX while interactive fiction and home computers contest the Christmas shelf.

lead.headline: COMDEX Becomes Las Vegas's Biggest Show as IBM Compatibility Takes Command
lead.dek: More than 80,000 visitors and 1,400 exhibitors gather around a market increasingly organized by the IBM PC standard.
body: The computer trade has taken over Las Vegas. A show that began in the winter of 1979 with roughly 4,000 visitors has swollen to more than 80,000 attendees, filling the convention center and rooms in five major hotels. Its 1,400 exhibitors include 400 newcomers, with AT&T among the names making a first appearance.

Yet the loudest message is not a revolutionary new box. Contemporary reporting finds most of the machines on display to be variations on the IBM Personal Computer design. Future Computing analyst Portia Isaacson puts the trend plainly: “The architecture of the IBM PC has become the industry standard.” Compatibility is becoming the language in which makers court dealers and buyers.

That shift changes the character of the show. Software and marketing are displacing the hobbyist hardware experiments that once supplied much of the excitement. Elaborate multistory booths compete for attention, and a serious display can cost tens of thousands of dollars. Hewlett-Packard expects to recruit hundreds of dealers for its new desktop system.

Windows draw the strongest crowds. VisiCorp demonstrates Visi On joining word processing, financial planning and graphing on a screen divided into separate panes. The industry arrives without a singular hardware sensation, but it leaves a clear direction: the IBM-compatible marketplace, stocked with graphical software and dealer support, is becoming personal computing’s commercial center.

stories.headline: Interactive Fiction Turns the Floppy Disk into a Bestseller Shelf
body: TIME this week treats text adventures as a new kind of software bestseller: stories in which the reader types commands, questions suspects and redirects the plot. Its opening scene comes from Infocom’s Deadline, where evidence and contradictory testimony turn the keyboard into a detective’s notebook.

Infocom’s The Witness carries the idea into a 1930s Los Angeles murder mystery. A December COMPUTE! review finds a world assembled through prose rather than arcade graphics, asking the player to examine rooms, objects and alibis closely.

The genre also solves a stubborn commercial problem. A portable text engine can carry the same tale across otherwise incompatible microcomputer families. On a crowded holiday shelf, the floppy disk is becoming a place for authored worlds as well as utilities and scores.

stories.headline: Home Computers Move to the Center of the Christmas Battle
body: The home computer has become one of the defining gifts of Christmas 1983. Atari, Commodore, Coleco and IBM are fighting for attention with sharply different combinations of price, memory, storage and bundled peripherals.

Antic’s holiday guide puts Atari’s 16K 600XL at $199 and the 64K 800XL at $299, both with BASIC built in. The $449 Atari 1050 drive brings enhanced-density disks and DOS 3.0, while touch tablets promise drawing and a more direct way to work on screen.

Coleco’s Adam counters with a bundled computer, data drive and daisy-wheel printer. IBM’s PCjr, announced in November but due to ship in early 1984, hangs over the season as a future entrant. Buyers are choosing not just a machine, but a family of software, storage and accessories.

stories.headline: Windows Become Software’s New Battleground
body: The busiest COMDEX demonstrations split a single screen into windows, allowing different programs or views to remain visible at once. Visi On places writing, calculations and graphs inside a mouse-driven environment for IBM-compatible machines.
The idea promises relief from the ritual of closing one task before opening another, but the price of admission is steep. Visi On demands an expensive, well-equipped PC by home-computer standards.

Even so, this week’s attention suggests that the next contest will not be decided by processor specifications alone. Software makers are now competing to define how people see, point to and move among their work.

issues.editorNote: Las Vegas is the center of the personal-computer world this week, and the message from the aisles is unmistakable: IBM compatibility is becoming a market of its own.
issues.morningLine: COMDEX opens, graphical desktops beckon, and home computers crowd the Christmas counter.

lead.headline: At COMDEX, IBM Compatibility Becomes the Winning Bet
lead.dek: The Las Vegas show reveals an industry rapidly reorganizing around the IBM PC standard.
body: Fall COMDEX opened in Las Vegas on November 28 with a floor full of machines, peripherals and promises. Yet beneath the variety ran a common current: makers were increasingly defining their products by whether they could work with the IBM Personal Computer and its growing software world.

The Washington Post put the trend plainly in its report from the show: “IBM Compatibility Grows.” That phrase captures more than a sales pitch. Compatibility offered buyers the prospect of choosing among vendors without abandoning familiar programs, disks and workplace habits, while giving smaller manufacturers a standard around which to build.

The exhibition itself had swollen into what a contemporary Christian Science Monitor report called the biggest computer show of its kind. The official show guide preserved by the Smithsonian records the scale and cast of this crowded marketplace, where add-on boards, printers, storage and software could matter as much as the computer case.

For home-computer shoppers, the same week still looked more fractured and price-conscious. But in business computing, COMDEX made the direction unusually clear: the IBM PC was no longer merely one successful machine. Compatibility with it was becoming the wager on which much of the industry expected to build the rest of the decade.

stories.headline: Windows and Visi On Put the Graphical Desktop in View
body: TIME’s November 28 issue described two software leaders giving computer screens a new look. VisiCorp’s Visi On and Microsoft’s newly announced Windows promised work arranged through graphical panels rather than commands alone.

Microsoft had announced Windows on November 10, and a surviving Fall COMDEX video documents an early demonstration. This was still a preview story: the commercial Windows 1.0 product would not ship until 1985.

The significance on the show floor was expectation. Software houses were asking buyers to imagine the personal computer as a visual workspace, with overlapping tasks and a pointing device changing how programs were selected and managed.

stories.headline: Holiday Buyers Enter a Crowded, Cut-Price Computer Market
body: The Christmas selling season finds home computers stacked against one another on price, software and promises of family usefulness. IBM’s newly introduced PCjr adds the biggest business-computer name to a field already defined by Commodore, Atari and other established home machines.

Low sticker prices may be welcome at the counter, but they also reveal the damage of the long price war. Post-COMDEX reporting suggests vendors expect the steep slide to slow in 1984, leaving shoppers to weigh support and software libraries alongside the bargain.

The PCjr remains more holiday conversation than broadly delivered product this week. Its arrival nevertheless reinforces the market’s central question: can a home machine borrow the authority and compatibility of the office PC without losing the affordability that created the boom?

stories.headline: Electronic Arts Mixes Chess Strategy with Arcade Action
body: Archon: The Light and the Dark turns a chess-like board into a field of direct combat. When opposing pieces meet, the contest moves from strategy to an action arena where reflexes can overturn apparent advantage.

The Free Fall Associates design is one of Electronic Arts’ first published titles and a vivid example of the new publisher’s pitch: computer games presented as authored creative works, packaged for a holiday shelf increasingly rich in experiments.

stories.headline: BYTE Asks Software to Become Easier
body: BYTE’s December issue carries the theme “Easy Software,” matching the week’s fascination with windows, pointers and friendlier screens. Usability is moving from a pleasant extra toward a central competitive claim.

The theme joins the trade-show story to the home counter. Whether the buyer is considering an IBM-compatible office machine or a family computer, the winning system may be the one that asks less ceremony before useful work begins.

milestone.title: Microsoft's Windows reaches the computer press
milestone.note: The November 21 InfoWorld demonstration captured Microsoft's first public bid to make a graphical, mouse-driven layer a standard across MS-DOS personal computers.

issues.editorNote: A mouse, overlapping panels and a common face for DOS programs point toward a different kind of personal-computer desk.
issues.morningLine: Microsoft opens a window on the DOS world while Thanksgiving shoppers confront a bruising home-computer price war.

lead.headline: Microsoft Opens a Window on the DOS Desktop
lead.dek: The newly announced graphical environment promises one mouse-driven face across the expanding MS-DOS market—but Microsoft is still showing a future product, not shipping one.
lead.confidence: Exact-date milestone; announcement November 10 and illustrated in the November 21 InfoWorld.
body: Microsoft has put a name and a visible face on its plan for the next stage of MS-DOS computing. Windows, announced in New York on November 10 and pictured for readers in this week’s InfoWorld, places menus, icons and movable on-screen panels between the operator and familiar programs. A mouse becomes a working tool rather than an exotic laboratory accessory.

The ambition is broader than a handsome screen. Microsoft wants a graphical environment that can travel across the growing population of DOS machines, collecting support from hardware builders and software publishers instead of belonging to a single proprietary computer. In an industry crowded with partly compatible systems, that common layer may be the most important part of the proposal.

Windows enters an active contest. VisiCorp’s Visi On is the immediate commercial benchmark, while other makers are pursuing their own graphical ideas. Microsoft says users will be able to move among applications and work through a consistent set of visual commands, a striking contrast with the command lines and memorized keystrokes now governing most desks.

Buyers should keep the calendar straight: Windows is a pre-release demonstration, not a box on this week’s store shelf. Microsoft projects shipment in April 1984. For now, the November display is a declaration of direction—an attempt to make the graphical desktop a standard companion to DOS.

stories.headline: Holiday Buyers Enter a Home-Computer Shakeout
body: The Christmas aisle is filled with bargains produced by a punishing price battle. TIME found one Atari home computer advertised in Los Angeles for $77.95, down from $630 three years earlier, while Commodore, Atari and Texas Instruments fought for volume at ever-thinner margins.

Texas Instruments has already announced its withdrawal from the home-computer business after severe losses. Clearance prices may delight shoppers, but they also raise hard questions about continued support, software and which machines will still have manufacturers behind them next year.

The cartridge-game crash deepens the uncertainty. Retailers are carrying discounted inventory, and publishers that once depended on dedicated consoles are looking toward home computers and rival platforms. The holiday bargain is real; so is the shakeout behind it.

stories.headline: IBM's PCjr Sets a $669 Floor for Big Blue at Home
stories.confidence: Same-month announcement; availability expected in early 1984.
body: IBM’s newly announced PCjr brings the company’s badge toward the family room at $669 for a 64K entry model. A $1,269 enhanced version adds 128K and a 360K disk drive, while color, sound, cartridge slots and a cordless infrared keyboard distinguish the small machine from its office-bred relative.

The Junior is not yet generally on sale; IBM points to the first quarter of 1984. Nor should buyers assume complete IBM PC software compatibility. Those cautions leave the holiday spotlight on the announcement itself and on whether IBM can stretch its business-computer authority into the fiercely priced home market.

stories.headline: Computer Chess Programs Learn to Outsmart One Another
body: Tournament programmers are setting computers against computers, turning the chessboard into a public test of search, evaluation and machine strategy. A November 21 Christian Science Monitor report follows the contests as programs expose one another’s weaknesses move by move.

Computer chess remains entertainment, experiment and demonstration at once. Every stronger performance gives home users a vivid measure of improving software, while programmers gain a demanding arena in which a bad assumption can be punished before spectators.

stories.headline: An Eyebrow-Controlled Computer Gives a Scientist His Voice
body: A paralyzed scientist in Nashville is continuing to communicate and work through a computer controlled by eyebrow movement, UPI reported November 22. The system turns a small remaining physical motion into selections and composed messages.

The achievement offers a humane counterpoint to this week’s retail battles. Personal computing is not only about speed, price or entertainment; carefully adapted input can restore a channel for thought and professional life when ordinary keyboards are impossible to use.

issues.morningLine: J.C. Penney backs away from Coleco’s Adam just as the Christmas computer contest reaches full volume.

lead.headline: Penney Drops Coleco's Adam From Holiday Line
lead.dek: A major retailer’s retreat exposes delivery and reliability doubts around the ambitious all-in-one home computer.
body: Coleco’s bid to turn its video-game success into a home-computer empire suffered a conspicuous holiday setback this week. The New York Times reported November 15 that J.C. Penney had omitted the Adam computer from its holiday line, a damaging absence at the moment families were studying Christmas catalogs and retailers were committing scarce shelf space.

Adam had been promoted as a complete household system rather than a bare computer: 64K of memory, keyboard, Digital Data Pack drive and a daisy-wheel printer in a package advertised near $700. That aggressive bundle promised word processing and home entertainment without the long accessory list attached to many rivals.

The promise collided with the difficult work of shipping reliable machines in quantity. Federal marketing approval had arrived in September and store availability was expected in October, so Penney’s November retreat sharpened questions about whether Coleco could meet the season it had spent the year courting.

The episode lands amid a punishing price war. Commodore and Atari are discounting established machines, IBM’s $669 PCjr has entered the conversation, and software libraries increasingly matter as much as specifications. For Adam, missing one retailer’s holiday line is more than a lost sale: it is a test of confidence in the whole package.

stories.headline: Microsoft Opens a Window on DOS
body: Microsoft’s newly announced Windows environment proposes a graphical layer for MS-DOS computers, bringing menus, a pointing device and multiple on-screen work areas to IBM-compatible hardware. The November 10 unveiling remains fresh news as the trade studies an early prerelease system.

The company’s broad compatibility pitch distinguishes Windows from graphical systems tied to one manufacturer. Bill Gates predicted rapid adoption across IBM-compatible machines, though both the software and the market still face a long road from demonstration to everyday desk.

stories.headline: Video Games Enter Christmas Under a Cloud
body: The cartridge business approaches Christmas carrying excess inventory, retailer caution and the shadow of Atari’s losses. Warner Communications reported a $122.3 million third-quarter after-tax loss in October as Atari’s fortunes collapsed.

Yet computer games are showing where players may go next. Ultima III, Archon and Lode Runner offer deeper strategy, construction and role-playing on programmable machines—experiences that dedicated consoles struggle to match.

stories.headline: Schools Add Ethics to Computer Literacy
body: A November 14 Christian Science Monitor report argues that students need values alongside technical skill. After the widely publicized intrusions by Milwaukee’s 414s, access to networks is no longer being discussed as a purely mechanical lesson.

Teachers and parents now confront a new question: how to encourage curiosity without treating an electronic boundary as imaginary. The debate signals that computer literacy is becoming a civic subject as well as a vocational one.

milestone.title: Microsoft announces Windows
milestone.note: The November 10 unveiling began the public history of the graphical PC platform that would later dominate desktop computing worldwide.

lead.headline: Microsoft Opens a Window on the PC’s Graphical Future
lead.dek: Bill Gates unveils a mouse-driven graphical layer for MS-DOS machines, promising menus, tiled windows and a common face for the compatible-computer boom.
body: NEW YORK, Nov. 10 — Microsoft this week unveiled Windows, a graphical operating environment intended to place menus, pictures and mouse control above the command-line face of MS-DOS. Bill Gates presented the product at the Helmsley Palace Hotel, giving the fast-growing world of IBM-compatible computers a glimpse of a more visual way to work.

The project began inside Microsoft under the working name Interface Manager. Its announced design combines pull-down menus, tiled windows, device-independent graphics and cooperative multitasking, allowing several programs to remain available within a shared screen environment.

Windows enters a field already being defined by Apple’s Lisa and VisiCorp’s Visi On. Microsoft’s wager is that a common graphical layer can span the many machines built around DOS, easing differences among displays, printers and pointing devices for both programmers and users.

The company is aiming for an April 1984 delivery, though the ambitious software remains unfinished. For buyers accustomed to typed commands, the announcement is still consequential: the largest supplier of microcomputer software has declared that the mouse and graphical desktop belong in the PC’s future.

Whether Windows arrives on schedule or wins immediate acceptance is uncertain. Yet this week’s demonstration has put a name on Microsoft’s strategy—and opened a contest over who will define the everyday face of personal computing.

stories.headline: A Self-Replicating Program Earns a New Name: Computer Virus
stories.dek: Fred Cohen’s controlled university demonstration exposes a new class of security problem.
body: At a Lehigh University computer-security seminar on November 10, graduate student Fred Cohen demonstrated a program able to attach itself to other programs and reproduce. The controlled experiment was academic research, not a public outbreak.

Cohen’s work gives the problem a memorable name—computer virus—and argues that shared systems can permit infections to spread with alarming speed. The demonstration adds a new concern to a year already filled with debate over unauthorized computer access.
The lesson is defensive: system designers must consider not only intruders but software that turns trusted programs into carriers. No operational code or intrusion instructions are reproduced here.

stories.headline: Computer Magazines Ride the Home-Micro Boom
stories.dek: Thick issues, machine-specific titles and type-in programs turn the magazine rack into a software shelf.
body: The New York Times reported November 9 on the explosive growth of computer magazines, a publishing boom fed by millions of new microcomputer owners seeking reviews, buying advice and programs.

General titles such as Byte, Creative Computing and Compute! share the rack with publications devoted to particular machines. Type-in listings make the magazines a low-cost distribution channel as well as reading matter.
Compute!’s November issue runs beyond 300 pages, its advertisements and product notices mapping an industry in which games, utilities and peripherals compete for the holiday buyer’s attention.

stories.headline: IBM-Hitachi Settlement Reported Near $300 Million
stories.dek: A reported secret pact underscores the value—and danger—surrounding mainframe compatibility.
body: A November 9 report said Hitachi agreed to pay IBM about $300 million to settle litigation accusing the Japanese company of technology theft.

The dispute grew from an FBI sting concerning alleged acquisition of IBM computer secrets. Its reported price shows how fiercely mainframe makers guard the engineering knowledge behind compatible systems.

lead.headline: IBM Cracks Open 'Peanut' and Sends PCjr Into the Home
lead.dek: The world's largest computer maker formally entered the home-computer contest on November 1, aiming above low-cost rivals while extending IBM PC software compatibility.
body: NEW YORK—After months of speculation about a machine code-named “Peanut,” International Business Machines formally unveiled the PCjr on November 1. The announcement puts the company that defined the business-PC standard directly into the crowded home-computer market, with deliveries planned for early 1984.

IBM priced a 64K system unit with a battery-powered cordless infrared keyboard at $669. A $1,269 package raises memory to 128K and adds a diskette drive. Neither price includes a monitor or printer; IBM's color display is $680, while a compact printer is $175.

The unusual keyboard can work from as far as 20 feet away. IBM cautioned that several PCjrs operating in one room would need cords to avoid infrared interference, a curious limitation for classrooms—one of the markets the company says it is pursuing alongside homes and small businesses.

Software compatibility may be the machine's strongest calling card. IBM said most programs written for the IBM PC should run on PCjr unless they demand more memory, while cartridge support and television compatibility aim to make the junior machine friendlier in the living room.

The PCjr arrives above the bargain end of the market and accessories quickly lift the full-system cost. Still, IBM's entry changes the stakes: home computing now has the attention of the industry's largest name, and every rival will have to answer it.

stories.headline: Apple II Gets an Arcade Board
stories.dek: A $225 expansion board promised coin-op-style graphics and sound while giving BASIC programmers more than 40 new commands.
body: Third Millennium Engineering introduced the Arcade Board for the Apple II, II Plus, and IIe. The board used many of the same video and sound chips found in coin-operated games.

It shipped with more than 20 demos, games, and utilities and extended Applesoft BASIC with more than 40 commands. The advertised price was $225. A $225 expansion board promised coin-op-style graphics and sound while giving BASIC programmers more than 40 new commands.

stories.headline: Activision Moves River Raid and Kaboom! to Atari Computers
stories.dek: Two best-selling cartridge games crossed from console to Atari home computers, illustrating publishers' push toward the computer-game market during the console downturn.
body: COMPUTE!'s November 1983 product pages reported Atari-computer conversions of Activision's River Raid and Kaboom!. The conversions were enhanced to use the greater capabilities of Atari home computers.

The news followed Atari's late-October move to publish games for competitors' machines, evidence of rapidly shifting platform economics. Two best-selling cartridge games crossed from console to Atari home computers, illustrating publishers' push toward the computer-game market during the console downturn.

stories.headline: Touch-Sensitive PowerPad Offers a New Way to Control Home Computers
stories.dek: Chalk Board's 12-inch touch surface represented an early consumer alternative to keyboard input.
body: The Chalk Board PowerPad was described as a touch-sensitive input device replacing the keyboard for supported tasks. Its active surface measured 12 by 12 inches.
COMPUTE! carried the product in its November 1983 news pages. Chalk Board's 12-inch touch surface represented an early consumer alternative to keyboard input.

issues.editorNote: Atari crosses old hardware boundaries while IBM and DEC redraw the line between desktop and host computing.
issues.morningLine: Arcade hits travel to rival machines, Big Blue brings the mainframe to the desk, and DEC puts VAX power into a microcomputer.

lead.headline: Atari Takes Its Games to Rival Machines
lead.dek: The Atarisoft label carries arcade names beyond Atari hardware as the home-game business searches for software revenue.
body: Atari is loosening the bond between its famous games and its own machines. A New York Times report on October 27 described new Atari titles made to fit competing home systems, turning the company’s arcade catalog into a software line that could reach players well beyond the Atari 2600 and Atari computers.

The Atarisoft label gave the strategy a bright retail identity. Platform-coded packages—surviving Apple II editions, for example, wear red—let shoppers spot the version for their machine while the Atari name and familiar coin-op artwork supplied the attraction. The box, rather than the console, became the company’s new front door.

That shift matters in a difficult year for video games. Instead of demanding that a household buy Atari hardware before buying Atari entertainment, the publisher could earn from owners of rival computers and consoles. Arcade properties could be translated, repackaged and placed on many more store shelves.

The conversions will still be judged machine by machine: controls, graphics and sound differ sharply across home platforms. Yet the business signal is already clear. A great game can travel, and in the crowded autumn of 1983 Atari is betting that its software names may range farther than any single box beneath the television.

stories.headline: IBM Links the PC Desk to the Mainframe
stories.dek: The 3270 PC and XT/370 join local work with corporate host access.
body: IBM is bringing two worlds onto one desktop. The 3270 Personal Computer combines PC-class local processing with access to IBM 4300- and 3080-series hosts, and was described as handling as many as seven applications concurrently, four supplied by host systems.

The Personal Computer XT/370 goes further, fitting an XT with three specialized boards so VM/370 applications can be processed locally. Its hardware includes terminal emulation, 524K of added real memory, an Intel 8087 and two Motorola 68000-family processors, with as much as 4MB of virtual memory.

For corporate buyers, the promise is continuity rather than rebellion: familiar languages and procedures from the machine room, paired with spreadsheets and other personal work at the employee’s desk.

stories.headline: DEC Shrinks 32-Bit VAX Power Into a Microcomputer
stories.dek: MicroVAX I points departmental and technical computing toward smaller packages.
body: Digital Equipment Corporation has unveiled the MicroVAX I, described in the October 24 Computerworld as the first micro-based implementation of DEC’s 32-bit VAX architecture. DEC rated it at roughly 35 percent of the processing power of a VAX-11/780 and support for as many as eight users.

The system is aimed at industrial control as well as business and scientific work. MicroVMS, the real-time VAXELN environment and the Unix-compatible Ultrix accompanied the hardware news, signaling that the smaller VAX is intended as a platform rather than a single-purpose curiosity.

stories.headline: FBI Seizes Gear in Multicity Hacker Inquiry
stories.dek: Unauthorized access becomes a national law-enforcement and privacy story.
body: The FBI has seized equipment belonging to 15 alleged computer hackers in 13 cities, Computerworld reports. The sweep shows how quickly remote access and electronic trespass have moved from hobbyist circles into a coordinated federal investigation.

The same issue gives prominent attention to computer matching and privacy concerns. Together, the stories place two sides of connected computing in view: outsiders reaching systems without permission, and institutions combining personal records with growing power.

issues.editorNote: Info ’83 shows the personal computer growing into an office workstation, while Coleco brings its ambitious Adam bundle into the holiday home-computer battle.
issues.morningLine: Networks link the desks, Adam reaches the shops, and a new generation of computer games fills the shelf.

lead.headline: Info ’83 Turns the Personal Computer Into an Office Workstation
lead.dek: DEC combines word processing, personal computing and communications as software and small networks dominate the New York exposition.
body: Software announcements dominated the 10th International Information Management Exposition & Conference in New York, but the larger story was integration. Machines once sold as dedicated word processors were being recast as connected personal workstations, able to prepare documents, exchange files and reach an office network from the same desk.

Digital Equipment Corporation’s Decmate Office Workstation made that convergence explicit. Its $4,735 package included the system unit, monitor, keyboard, Easycom logon software and WPS Convert, tying word processing to personal-computing and communications tasks under a 90-day on-site service plan.

The network followed the workstation onto the show floor. General Binding’s Northnet linked System 9 desktop micros, printers and disks for $4,400 per workstation, with electronic mail available as an option. Wordplex’s $450-per-node Wordlink could connect as many as 16 RS-232C electronic typewriters to shared printers while documents continued to arrive.

Software also promised a friendlier conversation with large machines. Frey Associates showed Themis, a VAX-11 information system that accepted plain-English queries from a base vocabulary exceeding 900 words and could learn more. Info ’83’s crowded aisles offered a clear forecast: office computing would be connected, software-led and increasingly personal.

stories.headline: Coleco’s $700 Adam Enters the Holiday Computer Fight
stories.dek: A printer, tape drive and 64K system arrive as one ambitious family bundle.
body: With federal approval secured in late September, Coleco expected Adam systems to reach stores in October. Priced around $700, the much-advertised package joined a bruising home-computer market with 64K of memory, a Digital Data Pack tape drive, keyboard, daisy-wheel printer and productivity software.

Adam’s complete-computer configuration also carried ColecoVision compatibility, giving console households an expansion story as well as a new machine. The unusual design made the printer the computer’s power supply, so Coleco’s headline bundle was inseparable in practice—a bold value pitch carrying equally bold engineering risk.

stories.headline: Desktop Networks and Electronic Mail Move Downmarket
stories.dek: Small systems share files and printers without waiting for the mainframe.
body: Northnet placed a server station over a cable network of System 9 desktop computers and peripherals, while leaving stations able to make independent connections. Its 16-bit node doubled as a file server, bringing the vocabulary of networking to modest office machines.

Wordlink aimed at another installed base: electronic typewriters. Up to 16 RS-232C machines could receive documents and share printers at $450 per node. Together the systems made electronic mail and shared resources practical product features rather than distant promises.

stories.headline: Portable and Multiuser Micros Crowd the Show
stories.dek: Suitcase systems meet Unix and MP/M-86 multiuser desktops.
body: Manufacturers unveiled desktop and portable systems at Info ’83 even as much of the microcomputer trade held its announcements for November’s Comdex. Xerox had introduced a portable days earlier, evidence that transportable IBM-compatible computing was becoming a recognized category.

At the other end of the range, Philips showed a 32-bit multiuser supermicro compatible with Unix and its workstation line. A Rair MP/M-86 desktop supported as many as 16 terminals and peripherals, included 1MB of memory and listed for $9,750; Computer Transceiver offered a dual-processor system for $3,295.

issues.editorNote: Portable computing faces its first great after-sale test while modems bring both play and peril into the home.
issues.morningLine: This week: Xerox steps behind stranded Osborne owners, a battery portable promises ten hours, and computer games gain an auteur-minded publisher.

lead.headline: Xerox Service Lifeline Reaches Osborne Owners
lead.dek: A fallen portable pioneer turns to an industry giant to keep its machines working.
body: Osborne Computer Corporation, once the most visible name in portable computing, announced October 11 that Xerox would service Osborne products while the manufacturer operated under federal bankruptcy protection. The pact offers owners a measure of continuity after the company’s swift reversal left the future of its machines and support network uncertain.

For customers, service is more than a footnote. Portable machines travel, absorb wear, and combine a display, disk drives, keyboard, and power supply in a tightly packed case. Access to Xerox’s established service organization may keep working Osborne systems productive even as the company that sold them reorganizes.

The arrangement also marks a sobering turn in the young personal-computer trade. Osborne helped prove that a complete computer could be carried from office to office, but rapid competition and financial distress showed that inventive hardware alone could not guarantee a stable supplier.

Xerox enters the story from both directions this week: it is supporting the installed Osborne base while introducing a portable machine of its own. Buyers now have a new question for every dazzling specification sheet—who will stand behind the computer after the sale?

stories.headline: Xerox Sunrise Claims a Ten-Hour Workday
stories.dek: The 1810 pairs 64,000 characters of memory with rechargeable batteries.
body: Xerox introduced its 1810 Sunrise portable in coverage dated October 13, describing a battery-powered machine with 64,000 characters of memory. The company said its rechargeable batteries could operate for ten hours, a striking claim in a field where “portable” often still means a heavy computer tied to a wall socket.

The announcement puts endurance at the center of mobility. If the claimed running time holds in daily use, the Sunrise points toward computers that can accompany a full working day instead of merely moving between outlets.

stories.headline: FBI Raids Bring Modem Intrusion Home
stories.dek: Seized home computers put teenage electronic trespass in the national spotlight.
body: Federal agents seized the home computers of four Irvine, California high-school students on October 13 as part of a multistate inquiry into suspected electronic intrusion. A follow-up report described a nationwide wire-fraud investigation involving alleged entry into defense and payroll systems.

The reports give the home modem a new and uneasy prominence. The same communications links that let hobbyists exchange messages and play at a distance can also cross boundaries that owners and institutions are only beginning to define. The episode is certain to sharpen calls for computer ethics, clearer rules, and better passwords.

stories.headline: Electronic Arts Puts Designers in the Spotlight
stories.dek: Computer Gaming World examines Trip Hawkins’ publishing model as Archon and Lode Runner command attention.
body: The October Computer Gaming World devotes a feature to Trip Hawkins and Electronic Arts, a publisher presenting software creators with the prominence usually reserved for recording artists. The approach arrives as computer games become more ambitious in design and presentation.

The same issue gives substantial attention to Archon: The Light and the Dark and features Lode Runner, alongside Combat Leader and The Cosmic Balance II. Together they show a market expanding beyond arcade imitation toward strategy, construction, and distinctive authorial voices.

issues.editorNote: Acorn crosses the Atlantic with a school-minded BBC Micro package while compatibility disputes, lower-priced 16-bit challengers, and touch-screen ideas crowd the personal-computer desk.
issues.morningLine: The BBC Micro arrives in America, Spectrum owners meet a compatibility snag, and the IBM-compatible field gets more crowded.

lead.headline: Britain's BBC Micro Makes Its American Debut
lead.dek: Acorn aims its $995 package at U.S. classrooms, with teacher notes, networking ambitions, and a 50,000-machine production commitment.
body: Acorn Computer brought one of Britain's best-known educational machines to the United States this week, formally unveiling an American BBC Micro package priced at $995. The October 7 debut placed the machine directly into the contest for school computer labs, where Apple and other established suppliers already had strong positions.

The American configuration was described as a beefed-up BBC Micro, with connections for disk storage, speech synthesis, and Acorn's Econet local-area network. Two sets of teacher-training notes came with the package, underscoring that Acorn was selling a classroom system and curriculum proposition rather than a bare home computer.

Popular Computing Weekly reported that Wong Electronics of Hong Kong had been commissioned to produce 50,000 U.S.-market machines over the next twelve months, with the first units due to ship during October. That production target gave the launch weight beyond a cautious export experiment, though schools remained the primary audience.

Acorn also planned to convene American education specialists to review domestic software, promote the strongest programs, and point developers toward gaps in the catalog. The company still hoped families would buy the machine for home use, but its first American argument was clear: computing belonged in the classroom, supported by software, training, and a network ready to link desks together.

stories.headline: Issue 3 Spectrum Change Breaks Some Existing Programs
stories.dek: Sinclair blames undocumented programming practices as cassette-era assumptions catch up with owners.
body: Owners of the new Issue 3 ZX Spectrum found that some programs written for earlier machines could fail because a replacement chip changed the byte describing the cassette and earphone port. Personal Computer News reported that software houses had not been warned before affected machines reached users.

Sinclair told dealers that programmers had relied on unsupported, undocumented behavior and called the practice unprofessional. Whatever the technical merits, customers were left holding software that had worked on yesterday's Spectrum but not necessarily today's—a sharp lesson in how fragile compatibility could be in the fast-growing cassette market.

stories.headline: Sanyo's $2,100 Challenger Joins the IBM-Compatible Charge
stories.dek: An 8088, twin drives, color output, and bundled DOS sharpen the price contest around the PC standard.
body: Sanyo's 555 arrived in reports from the SICOB show as another direct challenge to IBM's increasingly influential personal-computer platform. The 8088 system offered 128K of memory, two double-sided floppy drives, a Centronics printer connection, 16-color video output, MS-DOS, and Sanyo BASIC; CP/M-86 was optional.

Personal Computer News put the British price near £1,400, while an October BYTE dealer advertisement listed a dual-drive U.S. configuration at $2,095. The exact bundles differed, but the message was the same: manufacturers were assembling capable 16-bit DOS machines around an emerging standard and competing hard on included hardware and price.

stories.headline: Hewlett-Packard Puts 'Magic' at Your Fingertips
stories.dek: The HP 150 senses a finger through an infrared grid surrounding its screen.
body: BYTE's October cover previewed Hewlett-Packard's HP 150 under its development name, Magic. The 8088 desktop ran MS-DOS but was not hardware-compatible with the IBM PC, and its most striking feature was a screen that users could operate by touch.

Rather than relying on a pressure-sensitive display, the machine placed infrared emitters and detectors around the screen to locate an interrupting finger. Paired with still-unusual Sony 3.5-inch rigid-shell disks, the HP 150 offered a glimpse of a friendlier desktop interface—one that invited users to point directly at choices instead of memorizing every command.

lead.headline: Atari Dumps Truckloads of Games in New Mexico Landfill
lead.dek: Cartridges and equipment from the El Paso plant are crushed and buried as the console market’s inventory crisis becomes impossible to hide.
body: Truckloads of Atari material rolled into the Alamogordo, New Mexico, municipal landfill this week, where workers crushed and buried cartridges and equipment shipped from the company’s El Paso plant. A September 28 New York Times brief fixed the disposal to this week, turning a grim inventory operation into the sharpest picture yet of the videogame business’s retreat.

The dumping followed a bruising year for the console trade. Retail shelves had filled with more cartridges than buyers wanted, price-cutting deepened, and Atari’s once-dominant position was squeezed by both home computers and a flood of uneven software. Whatever individual titles lay beneath the soil, the convoy itself testified to the cost of excess stock.

Atari described the buried goods as discarded material, but the scale invited rumor almost immediately. Later archaeological work would confirm that cartridges and hardware were among the debris. The contemporary record supports the central fact without relying on the legends that grew around it: Atari sent truckloads from El Paso to be destroyed in Alamogordo.

For computer and game shops, the lesson was immediate. Software could no longer be treated as an endlessly expanding aisle, and brand recognition could not rescue every cartridge. This week’s landfill scene marks the crash not as an abstraction on a balance sheet, but as physical goods reduced to rubble.

stories.headline: GNU Call Asks Programmers to Build a Free Unix-Compatible System
stories.dek: Richard Stallman names GNU — ‘Gnu’s Not Unix’ — and invites a network of programmers to help create a complete shareable operating system.
body: On September 27, MIT programmer Richard Stallman posted a startling proposal to the net.unix-wizards and net.usoft groups: he intended to write a complete Unix-compatible software system and give it away so that users could share and change it. He named the project GNU, a recursive abbreviation for “Gnu’s Not Unix.”

The plan reached far beyond a single utility. Stallman listed a kernel, editor, shell, C compiler, linker, assembler, formatter, spreadsheet and documentation among the pieces required. Compatibility with Unix would make the system familiar and portable while avoiding dependence on proprietary Unix source.

The announcement asked programmers for contributions of machines, money and code, but its larger claim concerned control: people using computers should be able to study, improve and redistribute the programs on which they depended. That invitation begins a project whose tools and principles will reshape software development.

stories.headline: Apple Cuts Lisa to $6,995 and Points Dealers Toward Macintosh
stories.dek: The pioneering graphical workstation loses $3,000 from its original price while Apple previews a smaller January machine near $2,500.
body: Apple told dealers that a stripped-down Lisa configuration would sell for $6,995, down from the original $9,995. The reduction acknowledged the difficulty of selling an advanced graphical office system at five figures; period reporting put Lisa sales at only about 6,000 units.

The company was already pointing toward its next answer. Time reported that Macintosh was planned for a January introduction around $2,500, bringing Lisa-derived graphical ideas to a much broader price bracket. The cheaper machine was not expected initially to run Lisa or IBM PC software, making its ease of use central to Apple’s gamble.

IBM’s advance was the pressure behind the reset. Dataquest figures cited in the same report put IBM ahead of Apple in the $1,000-to-$5,000 segment, reversing their positions from the previous December.

stories.headline: IBM’s Unannounced ‘Peanut’ Has the Home Market Guessing
stories.dek: Before IBM confirms a name, price or specification, expectations for its home computer are already moving the market.
body: A September 27 New York Times personal-computing column captured the industry’s fixation on IBM’s rumored low-cost “Peanut.” Dealers and competitors expected a machine aimed at homes, but IBM had not announced it, leaving every price and specification in the realm of informed speculation.

The rumor mattered because IBM’s entry could reset expectations for Apple, Commodore, Atari, Tandy and Coleco. Buyers faced a familiar choice: purchase a proven machine now or wait for the weight of the IBM name. Until an official unveiling, the most important fact about Peanut was the pressure created simply by its possibility.

issues.editorNote: Apple cuts thousands from Lisa while Coleco clears the last regulatory hurdle to put Adam into the holiday computer fight.
issues.morningLine: The graphical future gets a cheaper price tag, and the home-computer aisle gains a formidable new package.

lead.headline: Apple Slashes Lisa by $3,000 as Sculley Resets the Company
lead.dek: A stripped-down $6,995 configuration aims to revive the pioneering graphical workstation while IBM seizes the middle of the personal-computer market.
body: Apple Computer opened the week with a dramatic answer to sluggish Lisa sales: dealers were told that the $9,995 mouse-driven workstation would be offered in a stripped-down $6,995 configuration. The $3,000 cut followed new president John Sculley’s four-day tour addressing some 1,500 dealers in 25 cities, a public show of urgency from a company suddenly chasing IBM in the market it helped create.

Lisa’s graphical desktop and integrated office applications still looked like a preview of personal computing’s future, but the machine’s price kept it beyond many offices. Time reported that only about 6,000 units had sold and quoted a Crocker National Bank executive saying even $5,000 might only make the bank interested, not convinced. Apple was also preparing IBM PC program compatibility for Lisa, an acknowledgment that corporate buyers increasingly expected access to IBM’s software world.

The competitive arithmetic had changed quickly. Dataquest figures cited in the period press put IBM at 28 percent of the $1,000-to-$5,000 computer segment, up from 12 percent the previous December, while Apple held 21 percent. The Apple IIe remained a brisk seller and cost roughly $1,500 less than an IBM PC, but dealers were already bracing for IBM’s rumored lower-cost “Peanut” machine.

Behind the Lisa maneuver stood a smaller gamble. Contemporary reporting said Apple planned a January 18 introduction for Macintosh at about $2,500, carrying Lisa-derived ideas into a more accessible computer, though with less storage and no initial compatibility with Lisa or IBM PC programs. By Friday, Apple warned that quarterly earnings would fall sharply; its shares, once $63.25 in June, closed the week near $29.38. The company’s graphical vision was intact, but the market was demanding a far cheaper way to buy it.

stories.headline: FCC Clears Coleco’s Adam for the Holiday Computer Battle
stories.dek: The approximately $700 all-in-one package can finally head for stores with 64K, data drive, printer, and ColecoVision compatibility.
body: Coleco said Thursday that federal regulators had cleared Adam for sale, removing the last formal obstacle between the ambitious home-computer package and Christmas shoppers. The company expected the machine to reach stores for the holiday season, where its promised combination of computer, storage, printer, and videogame compatibility would be measured against Commodore and Atari.

The complete package was announced at about $700, with 64K of user memory, a proprietary Digital Data Pack drive, and a daisy-wheel printer. Adam could run ColecoVision cartridges, while an expansion version was intended for people who already owned the console. Earlier in September, Coleco and AT&T had also announced plans for home-computer and videogame services delivered over telephone lines, giving Adam a communications story as well as a game library.

stories.headline: Portable Computers Crowd the Road-Warrior Market
stories.dek: September’s machines range from suitcase-like CP/M systems to battery-minded lap-size designs.
body: BYTE devoted its September cover package to “Portable Computers in Depth,” evidence that portability had become a category rather than a novelty. Buyers could choose integrated screens, disk drives, and bundled business programs, but every design negotiated the same hard tradeoffs: weight, battery life, display size, storage, and price.

The familiar Osborne and Kaypro approach put a complete CP/M office into a case a determined traveler could carry. Newer battery-oriented machines pointed toward something closer to a briefcase companion. Period reviews and advertisements show a market experimenting in public, with no settled answer yet to what a portable computer ought to be.

stories.headline: IBM’s Shadow Lengthens Across Personal Computing
stories.dek: Apple’s price move comes as IBM leads the key mid-price segment and dealers await a cheaper home machine.
body: IBM’s rise now shapes nearly every decision in the personal-computer business. Dataquest estimates placed Big Blue at 28 percent of the $1,000-to-$5,000 segment, ahead of Apple’s 21 percent, a reversal achieved in less than two years.

Apple still had the popular IIe and was developing a simpler, lower-cost version, but compatibility had become a decisive sales argument. Reports of IBM’s cheaper “Peanut,” expected in October, threatened to carry the company’s name from the office into the family room. It would emerge as the PCjr, but this week dealers knew it only as the next pressure point.

issues.editorNote: EXTRA EDITION: The portable-computer pioneer that once seemed unstoppable seeks bankruptcy protection, while a new generation of truly lap-size machines and inventive games points ahead.
issues.morningLine: Osborne falls, Electronic Arts plays on, and portable computing sheds twenty pounds.

milestone.title: Osborne Computer declares bankruptcy
milestone.note: The September 13 filing ended the first great success story in portable personal computing and became the industry’s enduring warning about announcing replacements before they are ready.

lead.headline: OSBORNE CRASHES INTO BANKRUPTCY
lead.dek: The portable pioneer seeks Chapter 11 protection after demand collapses and suppliers are left owed $45 million.
body: SAN FRANCISCO — Osborne Computer sought bankruptcy protection September 13, a stunning reversal for the company that turned a suitcase-sized computer and a rich software bundle into one of personal computing’s first spectacular success stories.

The 24-pound Osborne 1 sold for $1,795 with a five-inch display, 64 kilobytes of memory, a modem, two 5.25-inch floppy drives, and software valued at roughly $1,500. The formula drove sales to about $70 million in 1982 and made “portable” a serious category rather than a laboratory curiosity.

But customers stopped buying the Osborne 1 while waiting for the announced Executive successor. TIME reports monthly unit sales plunging from about 10,000 in February to roughly 100 in April. The delayed new machine failed to arrive in time to replace the evaporating revenue.

Manufacturing stopped early this month. Four hundred workers were laid off, Adam Osborne resigned, and only about 80 employees remained as the company entered filing week with virtually no income and $45 million owed to suppliers.

The failure offers a brutal lesson to every fast-moving microcomputer maker: a promised successor can destroy today’s product before tomorrow’s is ready. Osborne made portable computing visible; its collapse now makes timing, cash, and customer confidence just as visible.

stories.headline: Shakeout Reaches Computers and Cartridges
stories.dek: Victor cuts jobs, Adam slips again, and Imagic layoffs show the boom’s harsher side.
body: Osborne is not alone in feeling the market turn. TIME reports Victor Technologies has laid off 350 workers and expects a third-quarter loss, while Coleco’s $600-to-$700 Adam home computer has slipped again, putting its Christmas arrival in doubt.

The contraction reaches videogames too. A September 17 New York Times brief reports layoffs at Imagic, the prominent independent cartridge publisher. Hardware makers and software houses alike are learning that crowded shelves and ambitious forecasts cannot guarantee demand.
The surviving firms will need tighter inventories, dependable delivery dates, and products that stand apart in a market suddenly less forgiving of delay.

stories.headline: M.U.L.E. and Archon Turn Rivalry into Art
stories.dek: Electronic Arts’ first wave mixes strategy, arcade action, and face-to-face competition.
body: Electronic Arts is making a persuasive case that computer games can be a creative medium. Dan Bunten’s M.U.L.E. turns an Atari space colony into a four-player contest of land claims, production, auctions, and supply-and-demand economics.

Archon: The Light and the Dark begins like a fantasy chessboard, then lets opposing pieces settle captures through real-time combat. The combination makes tactical position and joystick skill equally important.

Both games place human rivals at the center. The Atari 400 and 800’s four joystick ports give M.U.L.E. a living-room immediacy that solitary adventures cannot match, while Archon converts every encounter into a miniature arcade duel.

stories.headline: A Portable That Really Fits the Lap
stories.dek: NEC’s battery-powered PC-8201 points beyond the 24-pound luggable.
body: September’s Personal Computing calls the NEC PC-8201 a “lap-size portable computer,” language that draws a sharp contrast with the Osborne 1’s 24-pound bulk.

Positioned against Tandy’s Model 100, the battery-powered NEC suggests the next portable market may belong in a briefcase and operate away from a wall socket. Portability is shifting from a handle on a heavy case to a machine that can travel as naturally as papers.

issues.editorNote: EXTRA EDITION: IBM compatibility is turning a crowded personal-computer boom into an industry standard—and a brutal test of which makers can survive.
issues.morningLine: Big Blue sets the standard, telephone lines promise games and software, and personal computers enter the drafting room.

lead.headline: BIG BLUE SETS THE STANDARD
lead.dek: IBM compatibility redraws the personal-computer map as a booming market enters its first great shakeout.
body: NEW YORK — The personal-computer business has reached the moment when a boom begins to choose its standard. TIME's September 5 survey reports that IBM, only two years after introducing its Personal Computer, has captured 26 percent of unit sales and displaced Apple from first place.

The market remains enormous and unruly: more than 200 American companies now manufacture personal computers, twice the number of two years ago, while 1983 sales are forecast at seven million machines. Yet the center of gravity is unmistakable. About 20 companies already make IBM-compatible systems, and buyers increasingly measure a new machine by the software, dealers, and accessories it shares with Big Blue.

That rush toward compatibility is exposing weak balance sheets. Vector Graphic turned a $2.4 million profit into a $3 million loss and laid off one-quarter of its 400 workers. Victor Technologies lost $11 million in the second quarter and eliminated 350 jobs; Fortune Systems watched an $8 million sales decline turn a $3 million profit into a $3 million loss.

Home-computer makers feel the squeeze as well. TIME says Timex Sinclair 1000 sales fell as much as 50 percent in two months even after its price dropped from $99 to $49.95, while Atari, Texas Instruments, and Mattel absorbed heavy losses. Rumors now point to IBM's own lower-priced home machine, code-named Peanut.

The lesson is no longer merely how to build a clever microcomputer. Compatibility, distribution, production capacity, and the timing of a successor model now decide who can remain in the game. The open frontier is becoming an industry—and IBM has planted its flag at the center.

stories.headline: Games by Telephone Move Closer to Home
stories.dek: Coleco and AT&T propose computer and video-game services delivered over ordinary phone lines.
body: HARTFORD — Coleco Industries and American Telephone and Telegraph announced a joint venture September 8 aimed at bringing home-computer and video-game use over telephone lines. The proposal joins the country's communications network to the fast-growing market for electronic entertainment.

The announcement arrives as Coleco prepares its Adam family computer, an expansion of the ColecoVision platform promoted with 64K of user memory, Digital Data Pack storage, a daisy-wheel printer, and SmartWriter word processing.

Details of the service remain ahead of the hardware, but the ambition is striking: programs and play need not remain sealed inside a cartridge or disk. The telephone may become a road connecting home machines to distant services and other players.

stories.headline: Draft-Aide Puts CAD on the Personal Computer
stories.dek: A five-level drafting line brings specialist design work toward smaller systems.
body: NEW YORK — United Networking Systems introduced its Draft-Aide line September 7 for personal computers as well as larger systems. Five user levels promise to scale computer-aided drafting to different needs.

CAD has long suggested costly specialist equipment. A product family meant to reach personal computers strengthens the microcomputer's case as a practical drawing and design tool, not merely a machine for ledgers, letters, and games.

stories.headline: Young Computer Experts Teach the Teachers
stories.dek: At Stanford, early-teen specialists help nearly 200 educators catch up with a new generation.
body: PALO ALTO — Computer-literate youngsters in their early teens helped instruct educators during a five-week Stanford University training course reported September 11. Nearly 200 teachers and administrators from around the world attended.

The reversal is a vivid sign of the home-computer era. Pupils who learned by exploring machines at home can arrive in class ahead of professional teachers, forcing schools to rethink who holds expertise and how quickly a curriculum can change.
