lead.headline: IBM's PC Standard Tightens Its Grip
lead.dek: The two-year-old IBM PC has taken the sales lead, inspired a compatible-machine industry, and left once-hot independents scrambling for position.
body: NEW YORK — The personal-computer trade has rarely moved so quickly from open field to established order. TIME reports this week that IBM's Personal Computer, introduced only in August 1981, now accounts for 26 percent of unit sales and has displaced Apple from first place.

The market around it is expanding at a dizzying rate. More than 200 American manufacturers are competing, twice the number of two years ago, while 1983 sales are forecast at seven million machines. Roughly 20 companies already offer IBM-compatible computers, evidence that buyers increasingly prize access to the software and dealers gathered around one standard.

That concentration is exacting a price. Osborne cut its pioneering Osborne 1 from $1,795 to $1,295 after advance word of the Executive slowed current sales. Vector Graphic turned a 1981 profit into a 1982 loss and has laid off a quarter of its workforce; Victor Technologies reported an $11 million second-quarter loss and eliminated 350 jobs.

There are winners as well as casualties. Kaypro founder Andrew Kay has enjoyed an estimated $245 million paper gain after his company's stock offering. Yet the lesson from showroom to boardroom is the same: technical novelty is no longer enough. Compatibility, software, distribution, and the ability to deliver the next model without sinking the present one now determine who remains in the race.

stories.headline: Ultima III Makes the Quest a Team Affair
stories.dek: Origin's Exodus expands the computer role-playing form with four adventurers, tactical battles, and a richly furnished box.
body: A new fantasy epic is giving Apple II owners an unusually ambitious journey. Richard Garriott's Ultima III: Exodus replaces the lone adventurer of earlier games with a party of four characters, each chosen and developed to contribute different skills.

Combat now moves to separate tactical screens, turning encounters into contests of position as well as preparation. The change gives the party structure real purpose and pushes the computer role-playing game toward a more deliberate blend of exploration, statistics, and battlefield command.

Origin Systems also treats the package as part of the adventure. A cloth map and extensive materials make Exodus feel less like a bare disk and more like a boxed world, a standard other computer-game publishers will find difficult to ignore.

stories.headline: Portable Computers Crowd the Departure Gate
stories.dek: BYTE surveys a growing field of luggables as Kaypro prospers and Osborne struggles through a painful model change.
body: Portable computing has grown from curiosity into a category crowded with choices. BYTE's September cover package examines CP/M luggables including the Osborne 1, Kaypro II, Zorba, and Pied Piper I, machines that promise a familiar office environment in a case that can travel.

The business fortunes behind those handles differ sharply. TIME estimates a $245 million paper gain for Kaypro founder Andrew Kay after the company's offering, while Osborne canceled its planned offering amid slowing sales and trouble bridging the Osborne 1 to its announced Executive.

These are transportable rather than effortless companions: displays are small, cases are heavy, and wall power remains essential. Still, bundling a screen, drives, and useful software in one enclosure is changing what buyers expect a complete computer to be.

stories.headline: Cellular Service Moves Toward the Marketplace
stories.dek: Ameritech forms a subsidiary to offer cellular mobile telephone service in the Midwest.
body: CHICAGO — Ameritech announced on September 1 that it has organized a subsidiary to offer mobile telephone service using cellular technology. The parent of five Midwestern Bell companies describes the unit as the first of its kind organized for the new service.

Cellular systems divide a territory into small radio areas and reuse frequencies as callers move between them, offering a path beyond the limited capacity of conventional mobile telephone networks. The announcement arrives just ahead of commercial cellular service expected in Chicago.

The early handsets and car installations will be costly, and coverage will begin in selected cities. Even so, the organizational step signals that a long-demonstrated technology is becoming a consumer communications business.

issues.editorNote: The personal computer is leaving the lab. This week, Clarkson freshmen collect desktops as routinely as orientation papers, while families face a crowded and fast-changing home-computer aisle.
issues.morningLine: Campus computers, arcade animation, and a sub-$1,000 price war define the week.

lead.headline: A Desktop for Every Freshman
lead.dek: More than 800 new Clarkson students are to collect personal computers during orientation, turning a bold campus requirement into everyday academic equipment.
body: POTSDAM, N.Y. — More than 800 Clarkson College freshmen arriving Thursday will receive an unusual addition to the standard orientation packet: their own personal desktop computers. United Press International reported the distribution on August 24, as the college prepared to put a machine directly into the hands of every member of the incoming class.

Clarkson announced the program the previous October and described itself as the first college in the nation to require every incoming freshman to have a personal computer. The distinction is larger than a crowded computer laboratory. Each student is expected to possess a machine as a regular academic tool, available for assignments, calculation, writing, and experimentation.

The undertaking marks a decisive change in the place of personal computing on campus. Only a few years ago, many undergraduates encountered computers through terminals scheduled around a central system. Clarkson's plan treats the desktop machine more like a textbook: individual, immediate, and woven into daily coursework.

Questions of training, software, maintenance, and how professors will redesign assignments now move to the foreground. Yet the scale of the handout is itself the news. For this class, computer literacy will not be an elective pursuit on the edge of college life; it begins at orientation.

stories.headline: Christmas Computer War Crowds the Aisles
stories.dek: At least 17 machines debuted at summer CES, and COMPUT! expects 30 to 40 sub-$1,000 choices by Christmas.
body: The home-computer counter is becoming a battlefield. COMPUT!'s August survey counted at least 17 personal computers introduced at the Summer Consumer Electronics Show and forecast 30 to 40 machines priced below $1,000 by Christmas.

The range runs from minimal low-memory machines near $40 to elaborate systems above $1,000 with modems, speech, and disk drives. Coleco's Adam is the boldest all-in-one wager: an 80K Z80A computer, high-speed cassette storage, keyboard, daisy-wheel printer, word processing, Microsoft BASIC, and Buck Rogers promised for under $600.

Price alone will not settle the contest. Buyers must judge software, storage, compatibility, dealer support, and whether announced machines actually reach shops. The crowded field gives families leverage but makes every purchase a bet on which platform will survive.

stories.headline: Dragon's Lair Turns the Arcade into a Cartoon
stories.dek: Don Bluth animation and laserdisc playback give players a startling glimpse of a movie-like arcade future.
body: Arcade crowds are gathering around a cabinet that looks unlike the familiar fields of sprites and maze walls. Dragon's Lair uses laserdisc video to display lavish Don Bluth animation, then asks players to guide hero Dirk the Daring through precisely timed joystick and button choices.

Rick Dyer's Advanced Microcomputer Systems developed the game with Don Bluth Studios and Cinematronics. Its branching scenes offer only limited control compared with conventional action games, but the spectacle is immediate: a coin-operated cartoon whose hero lives or dies on the player's cue.

The attraction also exposes the technology's tradeoffs. Memorization matters, wrong moves end quickly, and laserdisc hardware is more elaborate than ordinary game boards. Even so, Dragon's Lair is the summer's clearest sign that Hollywood craft and arcade machinery are converging.

stories.headline: Atari Clears the Deck for XL
stories.dek: The 400, 800, and 1200XL give way to a new family led by the $199 600XL and $299 800XL.
body: Atari is replacing its established computer line in one sweep. The company has discontinued the 400, 800, and recently introduced 1200XL in favor of four XL models, a drastic reset during the fiercest home-computer price competition yet.

The 16K 600XL is listed at $199 and can expand to 64K; the 64K 800XL is $299. Both build BASIC into ROM, retain compatibility with most earlier Atari software and peripherals, and expose a full processor bus for expansion.

Atari is also looking beyond its own hardware. A new publishing arm plans software for Commodore and Texas Instruments computers, acknowledging that popular programs may have to travel wherever the customers are.

issues.editorNote: Graphical computing is leaving the laboratory and meeting the hard questions of software, speed and developer choice, while imaginative games stretch the home computer in other directions.
issues.morningLine: This week in 1983: Lisa developers weigh their tools, M.U.L.E. and Suspended show new game ambitions, and Hurricane Alicia strikes Texas.

lead.headline: Apple Developers Confront the Lisa Software Puzzle
lead.dek: At Apple's August gathering, independent programmers see faster unreleased software—but face difficult choices about how to build for the graphical machine.
body: Apple's Lisa has made the graphical office a commercial proposition, but the machine's future now rests with people deciding what to make for it. At a week-long Independent Developers' Conference at the Dunfey Hotel in San Mateo, programmers gathered to compare methods, inspect works in progress and learn how Apple's unfamiliar visual environment might become a software market.

The contemporary Lisa newsletter Signal attended Lisa Day on August 11 and found developers choosing among standalone, windowed and Toolkit environments. The choice was not merely technical: it shaped how programs behaved, how closely they followed Lisa conventions and how much work their creators would assume. Signal reported that many developers still seemed unsure which route best suited their plans.

There was encouragement on the demonstration machines. Signal noted noticeable speed improvements in software not yet released, an important sign for a system often discussed as much for its deliberate pace as for its friendly interface. QuickDraw author Bill Atkinson also recalled Steve Jobs pressing for the rounded rectangles that helped give Lisa's display its distinctive, approachable character.

The opportunity remained expensive. Signal relayed a trade-paper claim that Apple's planned 1983 production of 20,000 Lisas was sold out, while sampled dealers quoted Lisa floppy media at $70 for five or $120 for ten. The conference revealed both sides of graphical computing's next step: remarkable tools and a developer community still working out how to turn them into fast, useful and affordable software.

stories.headline: Computer Games Grow Up: M.U.L.E. and Suspended Lead the Summer
stories.dek: Strategy, economics and interactive fiction claim feature space beside wargames and adventures.
body: The July-August Computer Gaming World treats two striking new designs as events worth extended attention. Electronic Arts' M.U.L.E. turns settlement and trade into a competitive economic contest, while Infocom's Suspended places the player inside a science-fiction crisis managed through remote senses and carefully chosen commands.

The same issue ranges through Battle for Normandy and adventure hints, evidence that computer gaming is no longer a single narrow genre. Its shelves now hold simulations, strategic contests and literary puzzles—experiences shaped as much by systems and imagination as by reflexes.

stories.headline: A $16.95 3-D Space Game Lands on Timex/Sinclair
stories.dek: Softsync's Mothership brings a pseudo-3-D corridor and two-player action to an entry-level computer.
body: The inexpensive Timex/Sinclair software economy has a new arcade entry. COMPUTE!'s August new-products pages list Softsync's Mothership at $16.95 plus $1.50 shipping and handling, a cassette-priced invitation to pilot Starlight Fighters through a hostile corridor.

The game offers one or two players, three difficulty levels, on-screen scoring and a pseudo-3-D display. Its keyboard becomes a control panel as players steer around drones—a compact example of publishers finding spectacle in machines built for a mass, budget-conscious audience.

stories.headline: IBM's ‘Peanut’ Rumor Keeps the Market Guessing
stories.dek: Expected low-cost and Unix machines stir speculation, but neither product has been announced.
body: The industry is already talking as though IBM's next personal computer has a nickname. Signal records expectations of a September unveiling for the rumored low-cost ‘Peanut,’ a machine whose shadow is influencing home-computer forecasts before IBM has formally introduced it.

The newsletter also relays an August Datamation report about ‘Popcorn,’ a rumored 68000-based Unix workstation near $10,000 and aimed at Lisa in 1984. Both remain period speculation, but the chatter shows competitors expecting IBM to press beyond the business desktop.

issues.editorNote: The industry is arguing about two futures at once: a costly graphical machine that courts programmers, and a flood of cheap boxes fighting over the family desk.
issues.morningLine: This week, Apple gathers developers around the mouse while Atari and Coleco reset the low end for a make-or-break Christmas.

lead.headline: Apple Courts Independent Programmers on 'Lisa Day'
lead.dek: At a week-long developers' conference, Apple works to turn Lisa's mouse-and-window interface into a platform outside programmers can build on.
body: Apple spent this week trying to convince independent programmers that its expensive graphical computer, the Lisa, deserves their labor. At a week-long Independent Developers' Conference at the Dunfey Hotel in San Mateo, the company opened Thursday, August 11, as 'Lisa Day,' walking outside developers through the machine's unusual mouse-and-window way of working and the tools available to write for it.

The pitch is complicated by choice. Developers were weighing three distinct environments—a standalone approach, a windowed approach, and Apple's Toolkit—each with different demands and rewards. Demonstration machines ran unreleased system software that observers reported was noticeably faster than the shipping version, a hint that Apple knows the current Lisa can feel slow.

Some of the week's most telling talk was about craft. Bill Atkinson, author of the QuickDraw graphics routines, recounted how Steve Jobs pressed him to add rounded rectangles to Lisa's drawing code—the 'warm and friendly RoundRects' that soften every window and button on the screen. It is a small detail that captures Apple's larger bet: that how a machine feels can matter as much as what it costs.

That bet remains costly. One dealer quoted five Lisa disks at $70 and another ten at $120, and the machine itself lists near $9,995. The contemporary Signal newsletter, which attended the conference, relayed an August Datamation report that Apple's planned 1983 run of 20,000 Lisas had sold out, while treating the figure as a claim rather than confirmed fact.

For all the price shock, the conference framed Lisa as a software problem more than a hardware one. As Signal put it, 'a relatively small group of individuals, and not a large corporation, created the software that makes Lisa so special'—a reminder that in the summer of 1983 the graphical desktop is still an idea in search of programmers willing to build on it.

stories.headline: Atari Erases the 1200XL and Bets on Four New Computers
stories.dek: The 400, 800, and short-lived 1200XL give way to a compatible XL ladder starting at $199.
body: Atari has swept away its established home-computer line, retiring the 400, 800, and recently launched 1200XL in favor of four new XL models. Creative Computing's John J. Anderson, noting the 1200XL's compatibility and video-signal troubles, wrote bluntly that 'the Atari 1200 has been benched,' its production halted before the machine was permanently withdrawn.

The replacements begin low and climb. The 16K 600XL lists at $199 and expands to 64K; the 64K 800XL lists at $299. Both keep built-in BASIC, full-stroke keyboards, and compatibility with nearly all older Atari software and peripherals, and add a rear processor-bus connector for expansion. Higher up, the planned 1400XL adds a 300-baud modem and speech synthesis, while the 1450XLD adds a double-sided, double-density drive storing up to 254K.

More striking than the hardware is Atari's new willingness to publish software for rival machines, including Commodore and Texas Instruments computers. Industry analysts quoted by COMPUTE! called the move 'the most significant development of the year'—an admission that in a brutal price war, code may travel to customers that Atari's own hardware cannot reach.

stories.headline: Coleco's Adam Forces the Home-Computer Market to Scramble
stories.dek: A promised sub-$600 bundle of computer, tape drive, printer, and software raises the stakes before Christmas.
body: Coleco's Adam has become, in the words of COMPUTE!'s Tom R. Halfhill, 'the system to beat.' The company promised a complete Adam—an 80K Z80A computer expandable to 144K, a detachable 75-key keyboard, a high-speed 500K-per-cassette tape drive, a daisy-wheel printer, word processing, Applesoft-compatible Microsoft BASIC, three-channel sound, 32 sprites, two controllers, and Buck Rogers Planet of Zoom—for under $600. A $450 expansion was promised for ColecoVision owners.

The bundle reframes the whole argument. Where rivals advertise a keyboard and leave storage, printing, and software to a shopping list, Coleco proposes to put a usable system in one carton. Period coverage cautioned that the specifications were not yet final and that Adam was only promised for fall 1983, but the announcement alone reset expectations.

It landed in a market already straining. After Adam's unveiling, Commodore outlined a Commodore 64 package under $1,000 and Atari said a 600XL with a letter-quality printer could sell below $600. COMPUTE! projected 30 to 40 sub-$1,000 personal computers confronting shoppers by Christmas, calling the season 'the Christmas of the Computers'—and the next twelve months 'a make-it-or-break-it year' for established vendors.

stories.headline: Laserdisc Cartoon and a Colony Auction Headline the Summer Games
stories.dek: Dragon's Lair turns the arcade into a theater while M.U.L.E. and Suspended dominate the computer shelf.
body: The arcade sensation of the summer is a cartoon. Cinematronics' Dragon's Lair pairs a laserdisc with Don Bluth's film-quality animation, drawing crowds—and a premium 50-cent play price—even though its branching action is driven by timed directional inputs rather than true real-time control. It is the month's clearest sign that video games and screen animation are converging.

On the home computer, the season belongs to more cerebral fare. Electronic Arts' M.U.L.E., Dani Bunten's four-player economic strategy game, drew feature coverage in Computer Gaming World's July-August issue, which also put Infocom's cryogenic text adventure Suspended on its cover and reviewed Strategic Simulations' wargame Battle for Normandy.

Together the titles sketch a widening hobby: a quarter-eating spectacle in the arcade, and thoughtful, sometimes social software at home. In a week dominated by hardware price wars, the games are a reminder of what all those machines are ultimately for.

issues.editorNote: The home-computer boom is becoming a contest over what people can do together: play, bargain, program, and communicate.
issues.morningLine: This week, four joysticks turn an Atari into a noisy frontier marketplace while a wave of new machines crowds the fall starting line.

lead.headline: M.U.L.E. Turns the Atari Into a Four-Player Marketplace
lead.dek: Ozark Softscape and Electronic Arts mix land development, arcade action, and a live commodity auction into one unusually social computer game.
body: A new game from designer Dani Bunten and Ozark Softscape asks Atari owners to gather around one machine and build an economy together. M.U.L.E., published by Electronic Arts, supports as many as four players, with the computer taking any empty places, and makes unusually direct use of the Atari computer family's four controller ports.

Each colonist claims plots on the planet Irata and outfits mechanical M.U.L.E.s to produce food, energy, smithore, or the riskier crystite. The choices interlock: energy keeps production moving, food buys time, and smithore supplies new machines. A player who ignores the colony's needs can discover that private advantage is hard to sustain.

The market is the game's great piece of theater. Buyers and sellers move their figures toward one another in a real-time auction, testing prices while everyone watches. Between rounds, short arcade sequences and random events keep the balance unsettled, so arithmetic never entirely replaces reflexes or nerve.

Computer Gaming World's July-August issue gave the title feature treatment beside Suspended and Battle for Normandy. In a season crowded with new hardware, M.U.L.E. makes the strongest case that the home computer's future may depend as much on inventive shared software as on another memory specification.

stories.headline: Seventeen New Computers Crowd the Fall Starting Line
stories.dek: Coleco's bundled Adam and a showroom full of rivals intensify the fight for the family desk.
body: COMPUT! counted at least 17 personal computers introduced at the Summer Consumer Electronics Show in Chicago and predicted that 30 to 40 sub-$1,000 machines could confront Christmas shoppers. The range ran from minimal 2K machines near $40 to elaborate systems above $1,000, a display of abundance that also warned how little room remained for undistinguished newcomers.

Coleco supplied the sharpest retail proposition. Its promised sub-$600 Adam combined an 80K Z80A computer, detachable keyboard, high-speed 500K-per-cassette drive, daisy-wheel printer, word processor, Microsoft BASIC, controllers, and Buck Rogers Planet of Zoom. A $450 add-on was promised for ColecoVision owners.

The bundle shifts the argument from the price of a keyboard to the cost of a usable system. Printers, storage, software, and a familiar game all arrive in the box—on paper, at least—putting pressure on rivals whose low advertised prices require a shopping list of accessories.

stories.headline: Atari Sweeps Away Its Old Line for Four XL Computers
stories.dek: The 400, 800, and short-lived 1200XL give way to a new ladder beginning at $199.
body: Atari has completely restructured its home-computer line, replacing the 400, 800, and recently introduced 1200XL with four XL models. The 16K 600XL carries a suggested $199 price, while the 64K 800XL is marked at $299; both include BASIC and full-stroke keyboards while retaining broad compatibility with older Atari software and peripherals.

Higher up, the proposed 1400XL adds a direct-connect 300-baud modem and speech synthesis. The 1450XLD adds a built-in double-sided, double-density disk drive storing as much as 254K. Together the machines are Atari's answer to a price war that has made yesterday's range look expensive almost overnight.

Atari Publishing is also preparing software for Commodore and Texas Instruments machines, a striking acknowledgment that software can travel where hardware sales do not. The reset preserves the familiar Atari graphics and sound strengths while admitting that the company must compete at several price points at once.

stories.headline: C and Scientific Software Reach the Personal-Computer Desk
stories.dek: An exact-week science column and BYTE's C-language issue point beyond the household budget program.
body: The New York Times devoted its August 2 Personal Computers column to new software for science and engineering, evidence that specialized calculation and analysis packages are becoming a recognizable microcomputer category. The personal machine is being asked to serve laboratories and technical offices, not merely play games or balance a checkbook.

BYTE's August theme issue, The C Language, follows the same movement toward more ambitious work. Its coverage of compilers, portability, and applications brings a language associated with institutional Unix systems before a broad microcomputer audience.

C cannot erase the incompatibilities among Apple, Atari, CP/M, and IBM machines, but portable source code offers programmers a way to think beyond a single box. That promise matters greatly in a week when the hardware showroom seems to acquire another incompatible family every few steps.

issues.editorNote: Commodore sharpens Britain's home-computer price war while Mattel finally launches the Aquarius and Nintendo's new Family Computer brings arcade hits home in Japan.
issues.morningLine: The Commodore 64 gets cheaper, the Aquarius reaches the shops, and a red-and-white game machine begins its first full week.

lead.headline: Commodore Slashes 64 Price to £229
lead.dek: A £116 British price cut puts a 64K color computer into the fiercest part of the home-micro market.
body: Commodore has taken what Personal Computer News called a “scythe” to its British prices. Effective August 1, the recommended retail price of the Commodore 64 falls from £345 to £229, a £116 cut that moves the 64K color machine into direct contention with far less capable rivals.

The official date may be next week, but the battle is already under way. PCN reports that Lasky's and Dixons moved early with offers around £225. A computer with sprites, sound, color graphics, and 64K of memory is suddenly sitting in a price band crowded with machines built around much tighter specifications.

Commodore is cutting around the system as well as the keyboard. VIC-20 and Commodore 64 game cartridges are set at £9.99, while the shared single disk drive drops from £299.95 to £229. VIC-20 memory packs also fall sharply: the 3K pack to £19.95, the 8K to £29.95, and the 16K to £39.95.

The cuts display Commodore's manufacturing advantage at a dangerous moment for the trade. Too many home computers are chasing the same household money, and makers must now answer a machine that offers a large memory, strong game hardware, and a familiar name at £229. Dealers may celebrate the traffic; competitors must decide how much margin they can surrender.

stories.headline: Aquarius Finally Reaches Launch Day
stories.kicker: Toy Giant Enters the Micro Race
stories.dek: Mattel's delayed under-£100 home computer launches in Britain on July 27.
body: Mattel's long-awaited Aquarius receives its official British launch on Wednesday, July 27, roughly three months after Personal Computer News first tested it. The toy company's computer arrives with a Z80-family processor, a rubber chiclet keyboard, and only 4K of RAM.

That under-£100 price is meant to open the door, but the market outside has changed while Aquarius waited. Commodore's new price and the growing range of inexpensive British micros make limited memory and graphics harder to excuse. Mattel's retail muscle can put the box before families; software and expandability must persuade them to take it home.

stories.headline: Nintendo Brings the Arcade Home
stories.dek: Japan's new ¥14,800 Family Computer begins its first full week with Donkey Kong, Donkey Kong Jr., and Popeye.
body: Nintendo's red-and-white Family Computer, launched in Japan on July 15, is the month's most intriguing game machine. Its ¥14,800 price buys a cartridge console with two hard-wired controllers and hardware designed to reproduce bright, fast arcade action on the family television.

Nintendo has led with names players already know: Donkey Kong, Donkey Kong Jr., and Popeye. The early catalog is small, but the promise is unusually clear—Nintendo's own arcade hits without the trip to the amusement center. The machine begins its first full issue week as a bold test of whether arcade loyalty can build a living-room platform.

stories.headline: KoalaPad Makes the Screen a Drawing Board
stories.dek: A $125 touch tablet gives Atari owners a direct route from hand movement to screen image.
body: The KoalaPad is a small touch-sensitive tablet that can reproduce drawn or written images, move a cursor or object, act as a custom keyboard, and even serve as a game controller. Antic lists the package at $125 including graphics software.

Its importance lies in the gesture: instead of translating every idea through keys or joystick clicks, the user can point and draw. For classrooms, artists, and home experimenters, the tablet makes computer graphics feel less like programming and more like handling a familiar pencil or brush.

issues.editorNote: Extra Edition: one million Apple II computers mark a new scale for the home-computer age, while software publishers debate how cheaply the programs can be sold.
issues.morningLine: Apple counts to a million; Commodore prepares to cut the price of what those machines run.

milestone.title: Apple sells the one-millionth Apple II
milestone.note: On July 18, the Apple II family reached one million sales, a landmark for the personal-computer industry.

lead.headline: Apple II Sales Reach One Million
lead.dek: Six years after its debut, the expandable 6502 machine crosses a landmark that shows how far personal computing has moved beyond the hobby bench.
body: Apple Computer sold its one-millionth Apple II on July 18, giving the personal-computer business a round-number milestone few could have imagined when the original machine appeared in 1977. The figure belongs to the whole Apple II family, whose color graphics, expansion slots, and accessible design carried it from enthusiasts’ rooms into schools, offices, and neighborhood computer shops.

The achievement is also a victory for continuity. While rivals repeatedly introduced incompatible machines, Apple kept the 6502-based line recognizable and useful, allowing owners to build libraries of disks, peripherals, and skills. Thousands of programs and a broad dealer network turned the computer into a platform rather than a one-season appliance.

That installed base now feeds a self-reinforcing market. Software houses can justify ambitious releases because so many customers own compatible machines; buyers can justify the hardware because shelves are crowded with business tools, educational titles, utilities, and games. Expansion cards further let an Apple II grow with its owner instead of being discarded.

One million machines does not settle the home-computer contest. Commodore’s aggressive prices and the swelling ranks of lower-cost systems are changing shoppers’ expectations. But this week’s milestone confirms that the personal computer has become a durable mass-market category—and that software may be the next battleground.

stories.headline: Commodore Threatens to Halve Software Prices
stories.dek: The hardware price war may be coming to cartridges and disks.
body: Personal Computer News reports that Commodore is pressing for a $99 ceiling on software and considering mass-market cartridges priced as low as $10 to $15. Such figures would cut sharply against premium packages and extend Commodore’s familiar hardware tactics into publishing.

Lower prices could put more titles into ordinary retail channels and tempt owners to buy more often, but they would also squeeze developers and dealers. The proposal makes clear that the contest for home-computer buyers will be fought as much on software shelves as at the hardware counter.

stories.headline: Whole Earth Maps a 40,000-Program Jungle
stories.dek: Stewart Brand turns cataloging instincts toward an exploding, confusing market.
body: TIME describes Stewart Brand’s effort to bring order to a software market estimated at roughly 40,000 programs. His Whole Earth Software Catalog would mix descriptions, criticism, and practical recommendations for buyers facing a bewildering range of products.

Brand planned to tap dial-up communities, including EIES, for recommendations—an early sign that computer networks could become engines of software word of mouth. The project recognizes a new industry problem: abundance has arrived faster than trustworthy guidance.

stories.headline: More Memory for Less in the Home-Computer War
stories.dek: Sub-$100 machines and rumors of IBM’s “Peanut” crowd the summer market.
body: COMPUTE! surveys a market in which falling prices no longer mean toy specifications. Commodore’s pressure and new Atari models are forcing makers to offer more memory and capability at prices that would have seemed impossible only a short time ago.

The magazine also relays expectations of an IBM home machine near $600. That “Peanut” remains rumor—the PCjr will not be announced until November—but its prominence shows how seriously established computer companies now regard the household buyer.

issues.editorNote: EXTRA EDITION: Japan’s cartridge-console contest begins in earnest, while home-computer players trade resources, paint by touch and command robots through a crisis.
issues.morningLine: Friday, July 15, brings Nintendo’s red-and-white Family Computer to Japanese shops with three familiar arcade names ready to play at home.

milestone.title: Nintendo launches the Family Computer
milestone.note: The July 15 Japanese debut created the hardware and software platform later exported as the NES, helping define the modern console business.

lead.headline: Nintendo Brings the Arcade Home With Its Family Computer
lead.dek: At ¥14,800, Nintendo’s red-and-white Famicom arrives with two controllers and three arcade conversions.
body: Nintendo launched its Family Computer in Japan on July 15, placing a compact red-and-white cartridge machine on shop counters for ¥14,800. The name was quickly shortened to Famicom, and the proposition was direct: swap a cartridge and bring the speed and familiarity of the arcade into the living room.

The console arrived with two hard-wired controllers. Its second pad carried an unusual microphone, while the initial software lineup leaned entirely on proven coin-operated hits: Donkey Kong, Donkey Kong Jr. and Popeye. Nintendo’s own history stresses cartridge changing and arcade-style play as the machine’s essential appeal.

That opening trio made the launch easy to understand. Rather than asking families to imagine what a new platform might someday do, Nintendo put recognizable characters and play patterns at the front of the counter from day one.

The week also finds Sega introducing its SG-1000 at nearly the same price, making Japan a testing ground for rival visions of the cartridge home console. The Family Computer would later be redesigned for overseas sale as the Nintendo Entertainment System; together, the Famicom and NES ultimately sold more than 60 million units.

stories.headline: Sega Enters the Living Room With the SG-1000
stories.dek: Sega’s first home cartridge system challenges Nintendo at roughly the same price.
body: Sega entered Japan’s home-console market in July with the SG-1000, a ¥15,000 cartridge system closely related to the company’s SC-3000 computer hardware. Its arrival put Sega within ¥200 of Nintendo’s new Famicom.

Early software included N-Sub, Mahjong, Congo Bongo, Yamato, Star Jacker and shogi. Historical accounts commonly associate the machine with July 15, though the surviving evidence makes the exact day less certain than the month; what is clear is that Sega and Nintendo began competing for the same living-room shelf in the summer of 1983.

stories.headline: Electronic Arts' M.U.L.E. Turns Economics Into a Multiplayer Contest
stories.dek: Dani Bunten makes supply, demand and bargaining the center of play.
body: Electronic Arts’ M.U.L.E., featured in the July-August Computer Gaming World, sends as many as four colonists to develop land and outfit mechanical M.U.L.E. workers for production. Food, energy, smithore and crystite become the raw materials of both survival and rivalry.

Its auctions turn economics into a social contest. Shortages, bargaining, collusion and sudden swings in supply are visible around the screen, giving Atari computer owners a multiplayer game in which reading the room can matter as much as reading the numbers.

stories.headline: Infocom's Suspended Puts Six Robots Between the Player and Disaster
stories.dek: A frozen overseer must save a planet through six very different mechanical senses.
body: Infocom’s Suspended: The Cryogenic Nightmare places the player immobilized inside a life-support complex while planetary systems fail. Commands must pass through six robots, each able to perceive and act on the emergency in a different way.

Michael Berlyn’s design turns limited information into the puzzle: the player must combine incomplete reports, dispatch the right machine and repair the system before disaster spreads. Its raised plastic face and elaborate documents also continue Infocom’s habit of making the package part of the fiction.

issues.editorNote: Coleco is betting that a computer, tape drive, word processor and printer can arrive as one family-room package. Meanwhile, arcades turn to animation and Electronic Arts gives designers star billing.
issues.morningLine: This week in 1983: Adam becomes the summer’s most talked-about computer, Dragon’s Lair draws crowds, and Electronic Arts’ first games reach reviewers.

lead.headline: Coleco’s Adam Promises a Complete Computer for Under $600
lead.dek: The summer CES sensation combines game compatibility, high-capacity tape, word processing and a daisy-wheel printer in one mass-market package.
body: The most talked-about personal computer of the summer is not merely a keyboard in a box. Coleco’s Adam, the lead item in the July 3 Arcade Express after its Consumer Electronics Show debut, is being pitched as a complete household system: computer, keyboard, high-capacity tape storage, word processing, joysticks and a daisy-wheel printer for a promised price below $600.

Inside, the Z80-family machine carries 80K of memory expandable to 144K, with 16K reserved for video. Its graphics system offers a 256-by-192 display and 32 sprites, while ColecoVision cartridge compatibility gives the newcomer a ready-made game shelf. Coleco also promises an expansion path below $450 for owners of its existing console.

The unusual piece is Coleco’s Digital Data Pack. Each proprietary cassette is rated for 500K, with transfer speeds claimed at eight to sixteen times those of conventional computer cassette systems. One drive is built into the package and a second was planned as an option. SmartWriter word processing lives in the system, making the bundled printer part of Adam’s identity rather than an accessory saved for later.

That integration is also the gamble. Popular Science cautioned that the demonstrated machines were prototypes, not tested production units, and Creative Computing singled out the proprietary tape format as Adam’s largest risk. A family buying into the package would depend on Coleco’s drives and media as well as its computer.

Even with those questions, Adam changes the sales-floor argument. Commodore can sell a bare 64 for far less, while Atari is bundling a writing system of its own. Coleco’s wager is that shoppers will pay for a computer that looks useful the moment the carton opens—and still plays the cartridges they already know.

stories.headline: The $600 System Becomes the New Battleground
stories.dek: Atari bundles writing tools while Commodore’s falling street price forces every home-computer maker to explain the whole package.
body: Adam arrives in a market where memory totals alone no longer settle the sale. Atari’s $600 Writing System combines a 600XL, AtariWriter, a guide, paper and a 20-character-per-second letter-quality printer, though buyers must still add storage and a television. Commodore 64 street prices, meanwhile, have been reported as low as $200.

That spread captures the market’s two strategies: sell the least expensive capable computer, or wrap the computer in enough useful equipment to justify a larger ticket. Mattel’s Aquarius and television offer joined the bundle race, while retailers marked down older Atari hardware with startling aggression. The result is a shelf crowded with packages whose similar prices conceal very different definitions of “complete.”

stories.headline: Dragon’s Lair Turns the Arcade into a Cartoon Theater
stories.dek: Don Bluth animation and LaserDisc branching give players pictures ordinary coin-op hardware cannot draw.
body: Cinematronics’ Dragon’s Lair, released to American arcades June 19, remains the most conspicuous new cabinet of early July. Developed by Advanced Microcomputer Systems with animation from Don Bluth’s studio, it trades real-time sprite drawing for hand-animated scenes stored on LaserDisc.

Players guide Dirk the Daring with timed joystick and sword-button choices, sending the disc to the next success—or comic death—sequence. The limited choices are hidden by lavish motion and color. In a year of game-industry contraction, the cabinet is a premium bet that spectacle can bring crowds back to the arcade.

stories.headline: Electronic Arts Gives Designers Star Billing
stories.dek: M.U.L.E. and a striking first wave of games treat programmers like recording artists.
body: The July–August Computer Gaming World finds Electronic Arts’ first wave in reviewers’ hands. Dan Bunten’s M.U.L.E. turns settlement economics into competitive multiplayer play as prospectors develop land, outfit robotic workers and bargain over resources at auction.

Alongside it, titles including Archon, Axis Assassin, Hard Hat Mack, Pinball Construction Set and Worms? arrive in oversized, album-like packages that foreground their creators. Exact retail months vary in later catalogs, but the period magazine makes the larger shift plain: a new publisher is selling computer games as authored works, not anonymous cartridges.

issues.editorNote: An arcade laserdisc, a CES’s worth of new home computers, and a Hollywood film about modems all arrive in the same week — and the price tags are sliding while the programmers argue.
issues.morningLine: This week in 1983: Dragon’s Lair turns the arcade into a cartoon, Coleco promises an Adam for the family, and WarGames makes the modem a movie star.

lead.headline: Dragon’s Lair Brings the Cartoon Arcade
lead.dek: Cinematronics’ laserdisc cabinet turns Don Bluth animation into the year’s loudest coin-op, and the rest of the arcade is scrambling to keep up.
body: Just weeks after the June Consumer Electronics Show handed the home-computer business its next big products, the arcade answered with a machine that played more like a movie than a game. Cinematronics’ Dragon’s Lair, in arcades from June 1983, drove a Pioneer laserdisc player with a joystick and a single sword button, jumping between pre-animated scenes of a knight named Dirk the Daring rescuing Princess Daphne from the dragon Singe.

The animation came from a team that included veteran Disney artists, working in the studio of director Don Bluth. Instead of the sprite-and-tile world every other cabinet in the alley offered, players watched fully drawn characters move through caves and corridors. Each choice was binary and timed: hesitate and Dirk walked into a death that was already drawn for the laserdisc to play. The look borrowed the storytelling grammar of Saturday-morning animation, and the trade press took notice all spring.

That novelty carried a price. Operators commonly charged 50 cents a play — twice the quarter most arcade games still asked — and the cabinet itself cost operators several thousand dollars, the laserdisc hardware driving the price far above ordinary uprights. Players queued anyway, drawn by the same storytelling spectacle that the trade papers had been writing about all spring.

For a software business racing to prove that a home computer was a serious tool, Dragon’s Lair was a pointed reminder of how much charm a coin-op could still pack into a cabinet. Coleco, Atari and Commodore were about to spend the rest of the year fighting over the family room; for one summer week, the loudest computer in the mall had a sword and a laserdisc.

stories.headline: Coleco Pitches Adam as the Family Computer
stories.dek: A keyboard, a daisy-wheel printer, and a high-speed tape drive arrive bundled for roughly $600 — if the schedule holds.
body: Coleco used June’s Consumer Electronics Show to position Adam less as a computer and more as a household appliance. The system paired a Z80A-based keyboard with a Digital Data Pack drive, a daisy-wheel printer that doubled as the power supply, and SmartWriter word processing built into ROM, all advertised as one package near $600.

Adam could also dock a ColecoVision, turning the company’s hit game console into a slot-loader for the keyboard. That kept the existing cartridge library relevant and gave Coleco a story against Atari and Commodore: one buy, one family, one box.

stories.headline: Atari Resets Its 8-Bit Line with the 600XL and 800XL
stories.dek: New cases, built-in BASIC and a Parallel Bus Interface are meant to clean up the entry-level fight.
body: Atari announced the 600XL and 800XL at the June CES as the clean successors to the 400 and 800. The 600XL shipped with 16K of RAM and the 800XL with 64K, both built around the 6502-family chips and Atari’s ANTIC, GTIA and POKEY custom silicon. Atari BASIC lived in ROM, ending the era when owners had to slot a cartridge before they could type PRINT.

The XL cases also added a Parallel Bus Interface, keeping the serial peripheral bus for drives and printers. Analysts read the announcement as much about inventory management as about engineering: Atari was simultaneously trying to clear 400 and 800 stock while preparing a price-war line that would face Commodore’s 64 and TI’s sinking 99/4A.

stories.headline: WarGames Makes the Modem a Summer Star
stories.dek: Matthew Broderick’s lightman reaches a war computer by accident, and a generation of teenagers learns the word wardialing.
body: WarGames, which opened June 3, was still in wide release by the first week of July, riding a wave of coverage that put the words "modem" and "war dialing" on the front page of the culture section. Matthew Broderick plays David Lightman, a Seattle teen who uses a modem and a little war dialing to reach what he thinks is a game company and what is actually the WOPR military computer.

The film’s cleanest line belongs to the machine: "The only winning move is not to play." For a Computer Chronicle reader, the resonance was practical — the same summer, BBSes were multiplying, CompuServe was signing new customers, and the cost of a 300-baud modem had dropped below $200.

stories.headline: The Price War Bites the Family-Room Shelf
stories.dek: Commodore’s chip-owning advantage and TI’s repeated cuts are forcing the rest of the field to rethink the entry-level price.
body: Inside the same week that Coleco promised Adam for around $600, the wider market was sliding the other way. The Commodore 64, which had debuted at $595, was already showing up at lower shelf prices as Commodore used its ownership of MOS Technology to keep the silicon cost down. Texas Instruments kept trimming the TI-99/4A, the machine that had once sold for several hundred dollars now advertised well below $200.

For Atari, the XL line was a response as much as a refresh. For Coleco, the Adam target price was a bet that families would pay a premium for a printer in the box. The market was about to find out who was right.

issues.editorNote: Software is leaving the hobbyist shelf for the mass market, while Summer CES machines promise another fierce autumn in home computing.
issues.morningLine: This week in 1983: software learns the hard sell, Coleco unveils Adam, and Atari remakes its home-computer line.

lead.headline: Software's Hard Sell
lead.dek: A $1.5 billion industry learns packaging, promotion and hit-making.
body: Personal-computer software is becoming a packaged-goods business. SRI International projects 1983 revenue of $1.5 billion, after $1 billion in 1982 and $600 million in 1981, and TIME counts at least 230 producers chasing annual growth near 50 percent. The machine may command the showroom, but the programs now determine what owners can actually accomplish.

The new model has hits, stars and launch campaigns. Electronic Arts presents entertainment programs in album-like sleeves and promotes their programmers as “software artists.” Lotus spent $1 million over three months advertising 1-2-3, its $495 combination of spreadsheet, database and graphing tools, and TIME reports it has become the bestselling business program.

Distribution is scaling just as quickly. Softsel expects $70 million in 1983 revenue while moving more than 3,000 products to 1,200 outlets; it accepts fewer than eight of the 400-plus programs screened in a typical month. Software-only chain Softwaire Centre International has 26 stores, 13 more under construction, and roughly 3,300 items in each shop.

Price pressure is arriving with the wider audience. Commodore says it will release about 70 titles over the summer and sell its version of Microsoft Multiplan below $100, far under editions costing as much as $275. Buyers who once studied memory maps now confront brands, shelves and advertising claims—the unmistakable signs of a young industry becoming a consumer market.

stories.headline: Coleco's Adam Takes Aim at the Family Room
stories.dek: A complete computer, printer and fast tape system targets a price below $600.
body: The surprise of Summer CES is Coleco’s Adam, promised for fall as a complete system below $600 or as a $450 expansion for ColecoVision owners. The announced package combines a Z80A processor, 80K of RAM, a 500K proprietary high-speed cassette, detachable keyboard and daisy-wheel printer.

Coleco also promises word processing, two keypad joysticks and Buck Rogers: Planet of Zoom in the box, while preserving ColecoVision cartridge compatibility. Graphics are specified at 256 by 192 pixels with 16 colors and 32 sprites. Period reporting cautions that final specifications—and the practical meaning of promised Applesoft compatibility—remain unsettled.

stories.headline: Atari Clears the Deck for Four XL Machines
stories.dek: The 400, 800 and 1200XL give way to a lower-priced compatible family.
body: Atari is discontinuing the 400, 800 and 1200XL in favor of four replacements. The 16K 600XL is listed at $199 and can expand to 64K; the 64K 800XL comes in at $299, sharpening the company’s answer to the home-computer price war.

Higher models promise communications and office features. The planned 1400XL adds a 300-baud modem and Votrax speech synthesizer, while the 1450XLD adds a double-sided, double-density disk drive. Atari Publishing also says it will produce software for Commodore and Texas Instruments machines—a striking breach in the old hardware loyalties.

stories.headline: Programs May Soon Travel by Telephone
stories.dek: Retail experiments test electronic delivery without a disk on the shelf.
body: Tymshare is testing in-store electronic software delivery at four shops in the San Francisco area, TIME reports. Control Video plans to begin delivering game programs by telephone later in June.

The experiments remain small, but their logic is powerful: a retailer could offer a broader catalog without stocking every box and disk. For an industry struggling with duplication, inventory and thousands of new titles, the telephone line may become part of the software aisle.

lead.headline: Software's Hard Sell Becomes a Billion-Dollar Business
lead.dek: Commodore readies roughly 70 titles, Lotus buys attention, and software makers learn the arts of packaging and promotion.
lead.confidence: Exact-date reporting for announcements during June 13–19
body: Personal-computer software is becoming a mass-market business before shoppers’ eyes. SRI International estimates that Americans bought $1 billion worth of personal-computer programs in 1982 and forecasts $1.5 billion this year, growth fast enough to turn code once passed among hobbyists into a fiercely promoted consumer product.

Commodore supplied the week’s clearest sign of scale by announcing roughly 70 software titles for summer. Its planned version of Microsoft Multiplan, priced below $100, would undercut versions selling for as much as $275 and put a serious business program within reach of the enormous Commodore home-computer audience.

At the expensive end, Lotus 1-2-3 combines spreadsheet, database and graphing functions for the IBM PC at $495. Time identifies it as the bestselling business program after Lotus backed the launch with a three-month, $1 million advertising campaign—a budget that makes software look increasingly like records, books or packaged goods.

Electronic Arts is making that comparison literal, placing entertainment programs in album-like packages and presenting programmers as “software artists.” Retail is changing too: Software Centre International counts 26 outlets, with 13 more under construction, while experiments in electronic delivery hint that programs may someday reach buyers without a box at all.

stories.headline: Coleco's Adam Resets the Complete-Computer Price
stories.dek: A sub-$600 bundle promises keyboard, storage, printer, software and ColecoVision games.
stories.confidence: Same-month CES announcement; specifications subject to change
body: Coleco’s Adam was the hardware sensation of the Summer Consumer Electronics Show: a complete system promised for under $600, or $450 as an expansion for ColecoVision owners. The announced package joins a Z80A processor, 80K of RAM, detachable keyboard, high-speed 500K digital-data cassette and daisy-wheel printer.

Word processing, Microsoft BASIC, sound, sprites, controllers and Buck Rogers: Planet of Zoom round out an unusually complete family package. Contemporary reports caution that final specifications may change before fall and that Applesoft compatibility does not mean most Apple software will run unchanged.

stories.headline: Atari Sweeps the Deck for Four XL Machines
stories.dek: The 600XL and 800XL lead a replacement line built around lower prices and broad compatibility.
body: Atari is replacing the 400, 800 and recently introduced 1200XL with four XL computers while retaining broad compatibility with existing software and peripherals. The 16K 600XL is tagged at $199 and expandable to 64K; the 64K 800XL is listed at $299.

Both bring built-in BASIC, cartridge support, joystick ports, 256 colors and four-channel sound. Atari is also opening its architecture to accessory makers and creating Atari Publishing to sell programs for rival Commodore and Texas Instruments machines.

stories.headline: WarGames Turns Computer Anxiety into a Hit
stories.dek: The computer-centered thriller climbs in its third weekend.
body: WarGames earned $5,355,801 from 973 theaters on June 17–19, an 11 percent rise from the prior weekend. Its domestic total reached $22,260,427 after three weekends.
The thriller ranked fifth nationally behind Superman III, Return of the Jedi, Trading Places and Octopussy, carrying modems, hacking and computer-controlled catastrophe into mainstream conversation.

issues.editorNote: Summer CES puts complete home-computer systems—not bare specifications—at the center of the sales pitch.
issues.morningLine: Chicago’s summer electronics show belongs to a game maker’s ambitious new computer.

lead.headline: Coleco’s $600 Adam Steals the Summer CES
lead.dek: A complete computer, word processor, fast tape drive and letter-quality printer promises to turn a ColecoVision household into a home office.
body: The busiest conversation at Chicago’s June 5–8 Consumer Electronics Show begins with an unlikely challenger. Coleco, best known for ColecoVision, has unveiled Adam: an under-$600 home-computer package built around a Z80 processor, a full-size 75-key keyboard, SmartWriter word processing, BASIC, a Digital Data Pack recorder and a daisy-wheel printer.

That bundle is the point. Buyers accustomed to pricing a computer, storage unit, software and printer separately are being shown the whole desk at once. Coleco says existing ColecoVision cartridges will work, includes Buck Rogers: Planet of Zoom, and promises an expansion route below $400 for current console owners.

Inside, Coleco describes 80K of total memory and an “Adamnet” communications circuit coordinating the system’s processors. The proprietary tape promises far faster transfers than an ordinary cassette, while the printer is rated near ten characters per second. Additional drives are projected at $150 and tapes around $10.

The applause comes with an important reservation: these are show prototypes, not production machines available for a full test. Delivery, reliability and the real retail price will determine whether Adam becomes a family computer or merely the most memorable promise of CES.

Still, Coleco has changed the argument for the week. Atari and Commodore now face a rival selling a complete activity—writing, printing, programming and playing—rather than asking shoppers to assemble a system one peripheral at a time.
lead.confidence: Exact-week announcement; specifications and prices are period claims for prototype hardware.

stories.headline: Atari Answers With XL Computers and a Writing System
stories.dek: The 600XL and 800XL lead a refreshed line, while a $600 bundle makes word processing the competitive measure.
body: Atari’s June 5 announcement brings new computers, peripherals, video accessories and 28 games to the same Chicago floor. The 600XL and 800XL are positioned as successors to the 400 and 800, retaining the value of Atari’s existing software library while offering a cleaner route into the next generation.

Its $600 Writing System combines a 600XL, AtariWriter cartridge, guide, paper and a letter-quality printer rated at 20 characters per second. A television and cassette or disk storage remain extra, but Atari argues that separately useful components give owners more freedom to expand than an all-in-one package.
stories.confidence: Exact-week product announcement with period follow-up coverage.

stories.headline: Software Price War Breaks Out at CES
stories.dek: Cross-platform publishing and sharp price cuts make low-cost computers more useful.
body: The hardware contest is spilling onto the software shelves. Creative Computing reports Datamost Gentry programs for Apple and Atari at $14.95–$19.95, Synapse Showcase titles for VIC-20 at $19.95, and TI-99/4A cassette programs below $10.

Commodore announces 70 titles, Easy Script 64 below $50 and Multiplan for the Commodore 64 at a quoted price that falls toward $50 during the show. Atari, Mattel, Imagic, Activision, Parker Brothers, Broderbund and Sega are all widening platform support as publishers chase the expanding installed base.
stories.confidence: Same-week CES reporting published in a period magazine.

stories.headline: WarGames Makes the Home Modem a Movie Star
stories.dek: A teen, an acoustic coupler and a military computer carry dial-up culture into packed theaters.
body: WarGames enters its second weekend just as home computers dominate the CES conversation. Matthew Broderick plays David Lightman, whose password guessing and modem exploration reach a military system and turn an innocent search for games into a nuclear crisis.

The film ranks fifth for June 10–12 with $4.8 million from 843 theaters and $14.2 million cumulative. Its thriller machinery makes passwords, dial-up exploration and connected systems understandable—and alarming—to audiences far beyond the computer club.

issues.morningLine: Games get album covers, computers get briefcases, and WarGames puts dialing into the movies.

lead.headline: Electronic Arts' First Five Games Reach Players
lead.dek: A young publisher treats programmers like recording artists—and ships a remarkably varied opening slate.
body: SOUTH SAN FRANCISCO — Ten days before this week began, the small company called Electronic Arts made its first shipment. Its May 20 slate carried five titles—Archon: The Light and the Dark, Hard Hat Mack, M.U.L.E., Worms?, and Axis Assassin—out of a warehouse and toward computer stores. The boxes announced the company’s ambition before a disk was loaded: creators’ names appeared prominently, and the packages borrowed the scale and visual confidence of record albums.

The selection makes a case for the computer as a broad game machine rather than a single-purpose arcade substitute. M.U.L.E. turns settlement-building into a competitive economy in which supply, demand, land, and luck keep changing the table. Archon begins with the outline of a chessboard, then lets opposing pieces fight their own action contests. Hard Hat Mack brings construction-site timing and hazards to the Apple II, while Axis Assassin and Worms? push in still other directions.

Electronic Arts is selling an identity as much as a catalog. By placing designers in the foreground, the publisher asks buyers to recognize the people behind the software in the way music listeners recognize performers. That approach also gives the first five games a family resemblance without forcing them into one genre.

The first shipping day was hardly glamorous. Company recollections describe the whole crew loading boxes for hours; Nancy Fong remembered, “We all worked all day long,” while Bing Gordon joked that they were terrible warehouse workers. Yet the improvised labor sent out a lineup whose variety and presentation suggest where packaged computer entertainment may be headed.
lead.confidence: Same-month; EA records date the first shipment to May 20, 1983.

stories.headline: WarGames Makes Home Computing a Summer-Movie Star
stories.dek: A teenager, a modem, and a military computer carry a new kind of thriller.
body: WarGames opens June 3 with a home computer and telephone modem at the center of its suspense. Its teenage protagonist reaches a military system while looking for games, then discovers that simulated nuclear conflict can be mistaken for the real thing.

The picture earns $6,227,804 from 843 theaters on its opening weekend, ranking third behind Return of the Jedi and Psycho II. Whatever audiences make of its technical details, the film gives dialing, passwords, artificial intelligence, and computer security a place in the summer-movie vocabulary.
stories.confidence: Exact-date opening and weekend grosses verified.

stories.headline: Portable and 16-Bit Machines Crowd the June BYTE
stories.dek: Greater memory, new processors, and battery power widen the definition of a microcomputer.
body: BYTE’s June cover package surveys 16-bit designs promising more memory and stronger management of it. The featured field ranges from Digital’s Professional 325 and 350 to HP’s Series 200 Model 16, the Intel 80186-based Pronto Series 16, and Olivetti’s Z8000-based M20.

Portability is becoming a serious design claim. The battery-powered Gavilan Mobile Computer can be paired with an optional printer small enough to share a standard briefcase. The same issue also examines the NEC PC-8201, Tim Paterson’s account of MS-DOS, VisiCorp’s Visi On environment, and Digital Research’s DR Logo.

stories.headline: Modems Bring Computer Gamers Together
stories.dek: Telephone lines and organized leagues hint at a social future for home games.
body: Computer Gaming World’s May–June issue places modem gaming and a computer baseball league on its cover, treating remote play as a culture worth watching rather than a laboratory curiosity. Players are beginning to imagine opponents and teammates beyond the room containing the machine.

The $2.75 issue also reviews Computer Ambush, Close Assault, and Germany 1985 and advertises SSI’s Knights of the Desert. Strategy remains central, but the telephone line adds a new possibility: a game community assembled through computers before consumer online services become ordinary.
